content: Wir sprechen in diesem Kurs über die Radarrückstreuung, die immer dann eine Rolle spielt, wenn ich mit aktiven Radarsystemen arbeite. Das heißt, es wird durch meinen Sensor aktiv ein elektromagnetischer Puls generiert, erzeugt, ausgesendet, Richtung beispielsweise Erdoberfläche gesendet. Und am Erdboden oder auch über dem Ozean erfolgt die Rückstreuung des Signals und ein Teil der ausgesendeten elektromagnetischen Welle wird zurück zum Sensor gelangen und dort registriert. Das heißt, wir haben ein aktives System, welches aktiv elektromagnetische Impulse aussendet und nicht auf natürliche Strahlung angewiesen ist. Damit sind mehrere Vorteile verknüpft. Zum einen kann ich mir selbst ein solches System generieren und die Systemparameter festschreiben, sprich Wellenlänge, Polarisation, Einfallswinkel, Energiestärke und so weiter und so fort. Ich kenne mein System. Zweitens bin ich eben nicht auf natürliche Wellen angewiesen. Ich habe ein aktives System, was auch nachts funktioniert. Und ein weiterer großer Vorteil mit Mikrowellen zu arbeiten, also mit Wellenlängen, in dem Fall jetzt in der Radarfernerkundung zwischen X-Band um die zwei Zentimeter, momentan L-Band, aber auch bis P-Band irgendwann hochgehend, fast ein Meter Wellenlänge. Ich bin in der Lage und kann Wolken nahezu frei durchdringen und habe mit Wolkenbedeckung wirklich in der Regel keine Probleme. Ausnahme wären massive tropische Regenergüsse und kurze Wellenlängen. Dann werde ich hin und wieder Artefakte durch solche Niederschlagsereignisse sehen. Im Regelfall beeinflussen mich Wolken nicht. Also zusammengefasst, ich habe ein aktives System, welches elektromagnetische Wellen erzeugt. Am Boden erfolgt die Rückstreuung und das zurückgestreute Signal wird durch meine Antenne generiert. Und damit unterscheidet sich das System von vielen anderen Systemen, die passiv arbeiten. Beispielsweise optische Systeme, die die Reflexion des Sonnenlichts einfangen. Oder auch passive Radarsysteme, die im selben Wellenlängenbereich arbeiten wie auch aktive Radarsysteme. Jedoch in diesem Fall die natürliche Strahlung der Erdoberfläche aufzeichnen. Und in dem Sinne nicht von einem System abhängig sind, welches aktiv Strahlung generiert. Jedoch haben solche Systeme den Nachteil, dass die Menge der natürlicherweise zur Verfügung stehenden Mikrowellenstrahlung sehr gering ist. Und ich muss über große Flächen integrieren, um überhaupt ein messbares Signal zu erzeugen. Was dazu führt, dass ich nur mit sehr geringen geometrischen Auflösungen arbeiten kann. Ein weiteres Beispiel für ein aktives System wären Lasersysteme, die aktiv wirklich Laserlichtimpulse aussenden. Und auch dort das reflektierte Echo wiederum registrieren. Solche Lasersysteme werden in der Regel dazu eingesetzt, Entfernungen zu messen.

metadata.video_title: Das Prinzip aktiver Radarsensoren

content: Hello everybody, my name is Ronny, Ronny Hensch. I work for the German Aerospace Center close to Munich in Oberpfaffenhofen on machine learning, computer vision for Earth observation data and in particular for SAR data. And that's also the topic of the talk today, deep learning for Synthetic Aperture Radar or SAR for short. And I want to start with a brief introduction, what is SAR and why it's so exciting and then share a couple of examples how we can use deep learning to analyze or to process SAR imagery. So probably most of you are familiar with optical sensors, the cameras in your mobile phones, for example. So those are passive sensors. This means they rely on an external illumination source, mostly that's the sun. So part of the sunlight is reflected on the surface, the object or the surface of the Earth and then is reflected towards the sensor that is basically measuring how many photons of a certain wavelength are entering a certain pixel. Optical images is not the only example, there are also thermal images or radiometers and so on. Now active sensors are a little different. Active sensors do not rely on an external illumination source. Instead they come with their own source of energy. They emit an electromagnetic wave, a pulse. This is reflected on the surface, part of it is reflected away and part of it is reflected back to the sensor and they are measuring how much of this energy that they send out is backscattered towards the sensor. Now you can do this with light, then it would be a laser. A laser is sending out an optical pulse, a light pulse and then measuring the energy that is coming back. But you can also do this with other electromagnetic waves, for example radio waves or microwaves and in this case we are talking about radar. SAR is not the only radar technique, there are others, but in this talk we will mainly focus on SAR. So now what is SAR doing? Well as I said, SAR is really just a sensor that is mounted on a plane or a satellite, there are also other SAR systems, but this is what we will focus on since we are talking about Earth observation data. And this sensor is sending out a microwave pulse that is scattered on the ground. Part of it is scattered away from the sensor, part of it is maybe absorbed by the medium and part of it is scattered backwards to the sensor. And the sensor is measuring then how much of this energy that was sent out is received again and also what is the phase of this information, of this signal. And then we can combine all the echoes of multiple pulses that we have sent out to get a full image. So these images nowadays they look a little bit similar to optical images, you see one image on the bottom right of this slide. They are a little bit differently though, we will see some of the effects in a minute in the next slides. So this is maybe one of the disadvantages, they are a little bit harder to interpret for humans but also for machines. The big advantage though is that they are independent of the Sun. As an active sensor you can acquire image data any time of the day including the night when an optical sensor is useless. Since we are using microwaves we are also more robust regarding weather conditions. If there are clouds or maybe storm, an airplane with an optical sensor can't even fly. Even if you have a satellite that is of course going above the clouds you don't see the ground because it's occluded and so on. For SAR it's not really a problem because you can penetrate cloud, you can penetrate smoke, dust to some extent, maybe even vegetation if you use the right frequency of the microwave. The problem though with radar imaging is that in order to get a high resolution, and that is what we want because we want to see a lot of details in the images, we want to see small structures and small objects, you would need to have a really large antenna. Of course you can't really mount a big antenna on an airplane and you also can't really send a really big antenna into space. It's either not feasible or even if it's feasible it's far too costly. So here SAR is making a really smart trick. It's using a small antenna and then it's moving the small antenna through space. Since it's mounted on an airplane or a satellite it's really just the movement of this platform. Then all those low-resolution images if you want are combined to a single high-resolution image with a really big antenna. This antenna is synthetic, that's why it's called synthetic aperture radar. This technique is actually already quite old. So the first SAR image from space was done more than 50 years ago, nearly 60 years now. Nowadays we have a lot of different satellites that are taking much, much better images with higher resolution, with different properties. This list here is not exhaustive. The images that we acquired today look somehow like this. Those are images from the TerraSAR-X sensor, that's a German satellite built together from Airbus and DLR. You see here on the left-hand side a river system with mangrove forest. On the right-hand side you see a volcano. If you wonder what is the circular structure around the volcano, that's a national park where there's a lot of forest. Outside of the national park you have like agricultural fields and cities and urban areas and so on. That's why you have this circular structure. Now we also have a lot of airborne sensors, a lot of airborne systems where the SAR sensor is mounted on an aircraft. Again this list is not complete, but one of the examples is the FSAR sensor that is built up by my group at the DLR. This is quite interesting, a quite interesting sensor because we can acquire multiple of those SAR images in different frequencies where each has a little bit of different properties. It's fully polarimetric, what that means I will explain in a minute, and we have a really high resolution down to a couple of decimeter. So here you see a couple of images or visualization of the SAR data and as you can see it's quite close to optical images. So even if you're not trained for SAR, if you have never seen a SAR image, you can recognize this is agricultural fields, there's roads, buildings, individual trees and so on. But still in order to really understand all the finer details in the SAR image you need quite some expertise. One of the biggest problems in SAR is called speckle. Now imagine you have multiple small objects in one resolution cell. Resolution cell is an area on the ground that is then projected into a single pixel. That might be like rocks for example or different plants if you're over a vegetated area and so on. Now if these objects are hit by the microwave, each of them will create their own independent echo. But then all of those echoes are combined and interfere with each other and then the combined echo is measured by the SAR sensor. This is what I try to illustrate here with those blue arrows, right, so this would be the individual backscattering signals from the individual objects but then all of them are combined together and superimposed. And the final measurement, this is a red arrow, right, so the length of this arrow is the amount of energy that is measured by the SAR system and the angle of this arrow would be the phase of the wave that we measured. And of course this is a chaotic process. It's not really a random process because if you would be able to recreate this image with exact same conditions, same sensor, same position, nothing on the ground has changed and so on, then you would exactly get the exact same image back, right. This is different to noise in an optical image, right. In an optical image even if I have the camera at the same position, I take exactly the same image, the noise will still be different. Speckle will be the same but of course we are not really able to get the exact same acquisition parameters. The other thing is if you just move this slightly, right, then the geometric relationship of all those small objects will have changed very very much, right. So this means you get a very different signal, right, the amplitude will be different and so on. And this is what we see as something that looks like noise in the image. It's not really noise although a lot of people call it in this way and it's very often modeled like that but it's this random fluctuation in the amplitude that we are measuring, right. This grainy thing that we have in the image and this makes it really really hard for humans to interpret SAR images but also for the machines. And if you look at the face of the signal, right, it looks like here on the right hand side it's basically completely random. It's, as I said, it's not really random, it's a chaotic signal but there is no information in the face of a single SAR image. Other effects are foreshortening. Since with radar we are measuring distances, not angles, an optical camera would measure an angle, right. So the position where an object is shown on the image depends on the angle it has to the projection center of the object. Now for SAR we are measuring distances. So we send out the pulse and we are measuring the time when this echo is recorded again. And depending on this, you know, you place this information at a certain pixel position. This means that if you have elevated object like a mountain for example, the top of the mountain since it's elevated is already closer to the sensor than a point on the ground. And this means that the slope that is facing the sensor will be squeezed together in the image, right, and the slope that is facing away from the sensor will be a little bit extended. And if you increase the slope you will come to a point where you not only have foreshortening but layover. So layover means that multiple points on the surface have the same distance to the sensor and since we are measuring the distance all of those points will be fused in the same pixel position. So in this example here, the top of the building and the top of a tree and the point on the ground, they will all be in the same pixel. And you see this also in the image on the right hand side, which is again from TerraSAX over an urban area with a little bit of a cutoff of a 3D model. And you see those high-rise buildings that are stretching into the bay, right. It looks a little bit like we would see the facade that is facing towards us, same as in the in the 3D model. But actually what is happening is that the sensor is flying on the top of the building, so in the north if you want, and the buildings are falling towards it. So it's actually the other side that is facing away from it from the facade that we are observing there. And those are details that are usually quite confusing if you're not trained in SAR images. And the last effect I want to mention is shadow. That is something we also know from optical images. But for optical images the shadow depends on the position of the illumination source, right, the sun for example. For SAR images it only depends on the sensor position, right. So the shadow is always on the opposite side of the object where the SAR sensor is. So it's always facing away from the SAR sensor. So this means that for SAR images there's an inherent orientation. If you show a SAR image to an expert with some elevated objects like mountains or high-rise buildings or individual trees, if the resolution is high enough, then this person can directly tell you where the sensor was flying and in which direction the center sensor was looking. There are many different variants for SAR. I don't have the time to cover all of them, but one of them I want to explain very briefly. That is polarimetric SAR or pulsar for short. Now SAR is working with electromagnetic waves, right, microwaves. And as any waves this is an oscillation, right. So if this is a propagation direction of the wave, the wave is oscillating in all directions, right, perpendicular to the movement of the wave. Now polarization means that we're restricting this oscillation in a certain way. So for example horizontal polarization means that the wave can only oscillate in a horizontal plane. Vertical would mean it only oscillates in a vertical plane. There are other type of polarizations too, but those are the ones that are mostly used for SAR. Now what we can do is when the sensor is emitting the wave, we can for example enforce a horizontal oscillation or polarization. And then when we are recording the echo, we're only recording the part that is also horizontally polarized, right. That would be the first image. So the HH means it was horizontally polarized during emission and we only measured the part that was horizontally polarized during reception. But then of course you can also measure the other part, right, that is only vertically polarized. That would be HV. And then you can also send out a vertically polarized wave and you can do the same. So this gives us those four different images with slightly different properties. And then we can combine all of them into this false color image. So don't get confused by those colors here. They are arbitrary. They are kind of selected in a certain way. It can't be real colors, right, because we are working with microwaves and not with optical light. But usually we are choosing a coloring scheme that is putting forest in the green area for example, because it looks more natural to us. So just to summarize a little bit about this brief SAR introduction. SAR is an active sensor. This means we are independent of the sunlight. We can take images at any time of the day, also during the night. It's based on microwaves. This means we are more robust to weather conditions. We can look through clouds, through smoke, dust, to some extent through vegetation. We can look through ice and sand and snow as long as it's dry and so on. It measures very interesting things because the echo that we receive, it corresponds to the geometric properties on the ground but also to dielectric properties and other things that we usually don't have in optical sensors. We are measuring the amplitude and the phase. This is really important because this means in every pixel of a SAR image there is actually a complex valued number. That is complicated things because a lot of computer vision algorithms are designed for real valued numbers only. And we can have multiple polarizations. Then we talk about POSAR images. We can have multiple images that are taken from slightly different positions. Then we are talking about INSAR or differential INSAR or tomographic SAR, TOMOSAR. We can combine those things. For example then we have pole INSAR. So the two images that are taken from slightly different positions also have different polarizations. We can have multiple frequencies and so on. And then also SAR images, they are a little bit more complicated than optical images because there are a lot of properties that we don't know, we are not used to from optical images. It's a complex valued signal. I already said that it's a distance measure instead of measuring angles, which causes like layover and foreshortening. We have a sensor-dependent shadow, not an illumination-dependent shadow. And we have the speckle effect. And about the speckle effect I want to talk more in the second part of this lecture.

metadata.video_title: Deep Learning for SAR - Introduction

content: All right, so now I want to talk a little bit about how can we deal with speckle, right? If you remember, speckle was this random fluctuation in our intensity and phase where I said it's really hard for humans to interpret that because for us it looks like a very, very noisy image. And it's also very difficult for machine learning approaches to analyze the SAR image if it has a lot of speckle. So right from the start there were a lot of approaches to try to reduce speckle in an image with traditional image processing approaches. But nowadays, of course, we try to do the same with deep learning and it shows that deep learning is actually very capable of doing that. So what do we want? We have this SAR image with really strong speckle. You see this here on the left bottom corner. And we want to put this into a machine learning approach. And since this lecture is about deep learning, it will be convolutional neural network that is then producing the same image but without speckle, speckle-free image. So how do we do this? Well, traditionally you would have your desired target variable that would be the same image without speckle, speckle-free. You put the input image with the speckle into your neural network. The neural network is doing a little bit of processing, is hopefully creating an image that has already a little bit less speckle, right? And you compare this output with the speckle-free image by a loss function. And then this loss is back propagated through the network in order to adjust the parameters of the network to do a better job. Now the problem here is we don't really have a speckle-free SAR image, right? Speckle is not like noise in an optical image. If I have a lot of noise in an optical image, there are things I can do, right? I can increase the brightness, for example, I put more lamps on it or wait until the cloud is gone. I can also increase the exposure, right? And then I get a much, much better signal-to-noise ratio. I can't do this for SAR because the speckle in SAR is not really this kind of thermal noise. It's an inherent property of the imaging process, right? It works this superposition, the interference of those individual backscattered echoes of objects in one resolution cell. I can't get rid of this. So there are a few ways to work around this. And the easiest thing with what people started was they used optical images and then they added artificial speckle. We can do that because speckle is actually a very well understood phenomenon. We have very good statistical models that explain, given the true intensity or the true amplitude of a SAR signal and maybe the surrounding in a certain area, we have very good statistical models that tell us how the speckle would look like statistically. So we can sample from those distributions to generate artificial speckle. We can put this on an optical image and then we have an image with speckle and we have the speckle-free image. Of course, this is not really optimal because an optical image is not a SAR image without speckle, right? That's not really true. There are many differences between optical images and SAR images. Speckle is just one of them, right? But it's a good starting point, right? And this way we can train the CNN with a speckled input and the speckle-free output. And that means that hopefully the CNN is learning the processing that is necessary to get rid of this random fluctuation. And once this is done, you can apply it to the real SAR images. So this has been done a lot. There are a lot of different papers out there that are doing this in one variation or the other. But the problem is really this gap between your training data and the actually SAR data at the end. As I said, an optical image is not a SAR image just without speckle. You don't have foreshortening. You don't have layover. You don't have shadow that is always appearing in a certain direction and things like this. Nevertheless, it works quite well. So here you see the original speckled image on the left and in the middle you see a despeckled image by a traditional approach. It's not learning-based, but also works quite well. And on the right-hand side you see the output of the neural network that was trained in this way. Now a slightly better approach maybe, but increasing a little bit the requirements is that you don't use optical images, but instead you're using multiple SAR images of the same scene. So you have a temporal stack of images that were all taken from the same surface point on the earth. Now the assumption here is of course that nothing changed in between, right? That everything is the same, just the speckle is different. And if this is true, you can align those images and just temporarily average them. This will also reduce the speckle by quite a bit. Now we have now this speckle-reduced reference data and then we can train the network in the same way as we did before with the synthetic speckled images. This is nice because now we are really working with SAR images, but of course it only works if you have a temporal stack of images that you can use in order to reduce the speckle for the reference data. This has been done not only for single-channel SAR images, but for example also for polar metric SAR images. Here you see one example where you have your input SAR image. You have two networks. One is trying to estimate the speckle-free SAR image version, right? This is compared to the reference data and the reference data is again a temporarily averaged image. And then you have a second network that is trying to estimate the speckle. And then the assumption is if I combine those two, the estimated speckle and the estimated speckle-free image, if I combine those two, I should get the original input image back. And then you can train this network end-to-end and then you have a despeckling network for polar metric SAR data. And here you see some results. On the left-hand side there is original input data. Then there is a very old traditional model for despeckling, the extended-leaf filter. It works to some extent, but there's a lot of blurring going on. The next column is also a traditional approach, but a little bit more modern. Resolution got much, much better, right? Speckle is gone, but there's still a lot of fine details are blurred out. And on the last column you see the deep learning approach, where speckle is also reduced by a big extent, but the fine structures are still very nicely preserved. So this works, but again, it has this really strong requirement that you need a whole temporal stack of SAR images where nothing happened in between, so that only the speckle is different. Now the computer vision community came up with a very interesting approach to this. So in the computer vision community, denoising is also a big topic. And there is a seminal paper here, Noise-to-Noise, that showed that you can reformulate the optimization problem of a neural network. So how to adjust the internal parameter so that if presented with an input x, it produces a certain output y, can be reformulated in a way that you don't need to have the reference data anymore. The only thing what you need is a version of the reference data that, if you compute the average of all of those different versions, it gives you the actual reference data. So in the language of denoising, what you can actually do is, you don't need to have a noise-free image. The only thing what you need is another noisy image of the same scene. This is much, much easier. It's not a temporal stack anymore, you don't need to have dozens or hundreds of images. One other image is already sufficient. The only important is that the noise is not really changing the image content, so that the expectation is giving you the noise-free one. If you would average over all the noisy versions, you would get the true image out. That is the only assumption. And this really works well. So they have then applied this technique that is coming from the computer vision community to SAR images. They started again with optical images, added synthetic speckle, two times, so that you have two noisy versions of the same input image. And then they train a neural network to estimate one noisy version from the other. So one noisy version is the input data, and the network has a task to create the other noisy version. And it turns out that the network can't really do that. It can't really learn the noise. The noise is just random. So it can't really reproduce another noisy version. So what it will learn instead is the underlying version, the true image, the noise-free image. So once this has been learned, once the network is trained, you can apply it to your SAR data. And then you have a despeckled image with less speckle. So they started to do this with an optical database and then artificial speckle. But of course, if you have multiple SAR images of the same scene, you don't need to do this. You can directly work with SAR images. So in this example here that was done for SAR images of volcanoes, you have two images of the same volcano taken from the same position, but at two different time points. The assumption is nothing changed in between those time points, so only the speckle is different. And you try to estimate one of those speckled versions from the second speckled version. And the network can't really do that. It can't really estimate the speckle and create a new one. So it will learn a despeckled version. And for this image, the despeckled version looks like this. So it works actually quite well, and it really increases the quality of the image. But also here, you still have this assumption that you have at least two images of the same scene where nothing happened in between. This is a quite strong assumption. It's something we can do. But if you're looking at environments where things are changing drastically, it's still a very hard assumption. So the computer vision community moved even further. So instead of doing noise-to-noise, estimating one noisy version from another, the next approach was noise-to-void, where you only use a single image in order to do something like this. And here, the trick is that you take a patch, and you blind out the center pixel of this patch. You just copy another value there. So you're basically destroying the information that was contained in this pixel. And now the neural network has the task, given the patch, so given the surrounding area, reconstruct this one pixel value. So given the surrounding area of this patch, what is the pixel value in the center? So this is the task of this neural network. And since, again, the neural network can't really estimate, predict the noise, it will try to underrun the noise-free version. That is the best thing the network can do in this application. Again, they applied this to radar data. And this is a paper I really like a lot, because it's combining the knowledge that we have about radar. It's a very well understood and very well modeled signal, where we are in full control of the sensor. We know exactly what we send out, and so on. And we combine this expert knowledge with a machine learning approach, with deep learning. So what I mean exactly is, speckled data is statistically very well modeled. One way to model it is this distribution here. So given a certain image patch, what is the probability of a certain value in the center of this patch? The true value, not the speckled one, but the true one. So this distribution looks very complicated. And it actually is. In practice, it's not so useful, because it depends on two parameters, alpha and beta, that we don't know. Of course, we know the measurement. We know the surrounding values of this pixel we are interested in. That is something we measure, we have access to. But these alpha and beta parameters, we don't have. But if we would have them, we could actually estimate the true value of this speckle. This is the second equation at the bottom. So given alpha and beta, the equation to estimate this is quite easy. It only depends on the measured pixel value, the speckled one, those two parameters, alpha and beta. And L is another parameter from the sensor system that we also know. So if you would know alpha and beta, we could actually estimate the true pixel value, only based on the image data. But in practice, we don't know that. So now what they did here was to use this noise-to-void framework in order to train a neural network to estimate alpha and beta. So given an image patch, they trained a neural network to estimate alpha and beta that was maximizing the log-likelihood of the statistical distribution. Now when this network is trained, we can just apply it to new data. It will give us alpha and beta. And with alpha and beta, we can just plug it into this equation, and we get the despeckled version. So this is a really nice combination of the expert knowledge that we have about the SAR signal together with a data-driven deep learning approach. And it works quite well. So on the very left side, you see the original speckled input image. And on the most right column, you see the despeckled version by this approach. And everything else are reference methods. All right. And with this, I complete my second part, where we talked about how deep learning can be used for processing SAR images to increase the quality of the SAR images. Here was the example of spectral reduction. But of course, there are many, many other applications, too. But now in the last and third part, I want to talk about how to use deep learning to analyze SAR images semantically.

metadata.video_title: Deep Learning for SAR - Speckle Reduction

content: Wir haben gesehen, dass Radarsysteme durchaus hohes Potenzial besitzen, Bodenfeuchte zu bestimmen bzw. Bodenfeuchteindikatoren abzuleiten, weil es immer so sein wird, dass eine veränderliche Bodenfeuchte sich auf das Radarsignal auswirkt. Haben wir allerdings Vegetationsbedeckung und die ist in einem solchen Umfang, dass ich mit meiner Radarwelle nicht bis auf den Boden vordringen kann, habe ich natürlich Schwierigkeiten, die Bodenfeuchte abzuleiten. Selbst bei einer geringen Vegetationsbedeckung wird die Vegetation nach wie vor einen dämpfenden Einfluss auf das Bodensignal haben. Dies ist schlicht und einfach ein Grundprinzip in der Radarfernerkundung. Das muss soweit akzeptiert werden und dementsprechend wird es auch behandelt, indem man beispielsweise dezidierte Missionen ins Leben gerufen hat, die sich hauptsächlich mit der bodenfeuchten Ableitung beschäftigen. Diese dezidierten Missionen, das sind auch Weltraummissionen, die kombinieren aktiv und passive Radargeräte. Das Besondere bei passiven Radargeräten ist, dass die deutlich weniger beeinflusst werden von Vegetationseinflüssen. Die Kombination aus aktiv und passiv, dafür gibt es zwei Beispiele, SMOS und SMEP, diese Missionen wurden rein dafür gestartet, Bodenfeuchte abzuleiten. Der große Nachteil von passiven Radarsystemen ist die deutlich schlechtere geometrische Auflösung. Wir reden hier nicht mehr um Meter oder Zehnermeter, sondern die Auflösung ist in der Regel deutlich schlechter, Hunderte Meter, wenn nicht Kilometer Auflösung. Dennoch ist es für all diese Missionen wichtig, für die Validierung der Ergebnisse, aber auch für das Kalibrieren der Modelle, Referenzinformationen zu haben, also tatsächliche bodenfeuchte Messwerte am Boden. Man muss also ins Gelände gehen, die Bodenfeuchte ermitteln beziehungsweise die die Elektrizitätskonstante ermitteln und dafür gibt es zwei Hauptrichtungen, die da verfolgt werden können. Das eine ist ein sogenannter gravimetrischer Ansatz und das andere ein volumetrischer Ansatz. Da wir bei den Bodenproben Vergleichen zwischen Gewicht vor und nach trocknen, sprechen wir von der gravimetrischen Methode. Volumetrische Methoden sind beispielsweise die Frequency Domain oder die Time Domain Reflectometry. Bei der Time Domain Reflectometry wird entlang von Metallstäben, das kann ein Stab sein, es können mehrere Stäbe sein, elektromagnetische Impulse ausgesendet und die Laufzeit zur Stabspitze und zurück wird ermittelt. Diese Laufzeit steht in direkten Zusammenhang zur Elektrizitätskonstante. Wenn ich jetzt die Bodeneigenschaften so weit kenne, beziehungsweise eben meine Sonde für diesen Boden kalibriere, kann ich direkte Aussagen treffen, was die volumetrische Bodenfeuchte betrifft. Ein besonderer Fall bei der bodenfeuchte Bestimmung über Radarfernerkundungsdaten tritt dann ein, wenn eine Frostperiode auftritt. Durch die Frostperiode wird es dazu kommen, dass der Boden gefriert und Bodengefrieren heißt in dem Fall die Feuchtigkeit des Wasser im Boden gefriert. Gefrorenes Wasser hat eine deutlich geringere Dielektrizitätskonstante als die von flüssigem Wasser. Das führt dazu, dass das Epsilon stark nach unten geht, die Interaktion der Mikrowelle mit dem gefrorenen Boden reduziert ist und die Radarückstreuung demzufolge auch reduziert ist. Diese Effekte kann man sehr gut beobachten, wenn man mit Radarzeitreihen arbeitet und es wurde immer wieder festgestellt, dass tatsächlich Frostperioden auch per Radarfernerkundung zu detektieren gehen. Dasselbe wie für das Wasser im Boden gilt natürlich auch für das Wasser außerhalb des Bodens, sprich auf dem Boden in Form von Schneebedeckungen oder in Form von Eis auf Gewässern. Auch da hat das Wasser eine deutlich geringere Dielektrizitätskonstante als flüssiges Wasser. Das kann dazu führen, dass ich eine Schneedecke vollständig durchdringe und die Interaktion zwischen Mikrowelle, also elektromagnetischer Radarwelle und Bodenoberfläche genau an der Grenze zwischen Schnee und Boden passiert. Oder ein anderer Spezialfall ist, dass Eis auf Gewässern durchdrungen wird und die Interaktion an der Grenzschicht zwischen dem Eis und dem unterliegenden flüssigen Wasser passiert. Das ist wichtig, dass man versteht, dass Wasser je nach Aggregatzustand unterschiedlich mit den elektromagnetischen Wellen interagiert. Generell gilt der Zusammenhang, dass mit zunehmender Bodenfeuchte auch eine zunehmende Radarrückstreuung zu verzeichnen ist. Das hat aber nach oben hin irgendwo auch seine Grenzen. Und zwar dann, wenn der Boden vollständig gesättigt ist und es dazu führt, dass sich auf dem Boden Wasseransammlungen bilden, also größere Pfützen tatsächlich, kleinere Seen zum Teil. Wassersättigung, stehendes Wasser auf einem Boden und wiederum zu anderen Zeitpunkten tatsächlich nicht vorhandenes Wasser auf demselben Areal. content: Ein Parameter, der die Radarückstreuung dominant bestimmt für vegetationsfreie Flächen, ist die sogenannte Oberflächenrauhigkeit oder Rauheit. Während für den Fall einer sehr glatten Oberfläche, und das kann beispielsweise, wie gesagt, ein Saatspät sein, ein wirklich sehr glattes Feld, da kann es durchaus passieren, dass der allergrößte Teil der einfallenden elektromagnetischen Wellen eben weggestreut wird vom Sensor, und zurück zum Sensor so gut wie gar nichts kommt. Und wenn ich vielleicht überhaupt noch etwas messe, beziehungsweise selbst wenn ein geringer Anteil an Rückstreuintensität zum Sensor gelangen würde, könnte es sogar sein, dass es niedriger ist als der Sensor Neusflor, und ich nicht registrieren kann, dass tatsächlich Rückstreuintensität messbar gewesen wäre. Wir haben also für glatte Oberflächen meistens auch eine sehr, sehr geringe Rückstreuung und für raue Oberflächen eine deutlich höhere Rückstreuintensität. Wir müssen aber beachten, wenn wir hier von Rauigkeit sprechen, dass wir die Wellenlänge nicht außer Acht lassen, denn die Wellenlänge an sich definiert, was eigentlich rau ist. Während große Wellenlängen tatsächlich auch größere Rauigkeiten benötigen, um eine hohe Rückstreuintensität zu generieren, mag für kurze Wellenlängen auch eine geringe Rauigkeit ausreichen. Oder mit anderen Worten, für kurze Wellenlängen, beispielsweise X-Band, erscheint die eine oder andere Fläche vielleicht durchaus noch rau, während für lange Wellenlängen, beispielsweise L-Band, die Fläche bereits glatt erscheint und dementsprechend auch andere Streuprozesse hervorgerufen werden. Ein weiteres konkretes Beispiel, was aber ganz ähnlich funktioniert wie für Ackerflächen, sind Wasserflächen. Letzten Endes hat eine Wasseroberfläche, nehmen wir mal eine Meeresfläche, nur noch das weitere Spezifikum, dass wir es nicht mit einem Boden zu tun haben, sondern mit einem Medium mit einer sehr, sehr hohen Dielektrizitätskonstante. Und das selbst für glatte Oberflächen, wo im langwelligen Bereich, im oberen Bodenbereich vielleicht sogar noch ein bisschen Volumenstreuung stattfinden könnte, das wird für Wasserflächen nicht passieren. Das heißt, glatte Wasseroberflächen sind im Prinzip dazu prädestiniert, spiegelnd zu streuen. Mit anderen Worten, für glatte Wasserflächen werden wir in der Regel keine messbare Radarrückstreuung generieren können. Während für raue Wasseroberflächen sehr wohl sehr hohe Radarrückstreuungen generiert werden können. Diesen Zusammenhang machen sich viele Ozeanografen zunutze, indem über die Rückstreuintensität beispielsweise die Wellenhöhe oder vielleicht sogar die Wellenstruktur abgeleitet wird. Zusammenfassend können wir festhalten, dass für vegetationsfreie Flächen, und das können beispielsweise Wasserflächen sein, das können vegetationsfreie Böden sein oder auch Schneeoberflächen, Eisoberflächen, dass dort die Oberflächenrauhigkeit eigentlich die Rückstreuintensität dominiert. content: Ein weiterer wesentlicher Parameter, der die Rückstreuintensität beeinflusst, ist die sogenannte Polarisation. Und das macht man dementsprechend auch und man hat aufgrund der relativ einfachen technischen Umsetzbarkeit vorgezogen, mit sogenannten linear polarisierten elektromagnetischen Wellen zu arbeiten. Wenn wir uns jetzt mal rein nur den elektrischen Feldvektor betrachten wollen, einer elektromagnetischen Welle, gibt es eben die Möglichkeit, eine solche Welle horizontal oder vertikal zu polarisieren. Also wir haben es mit elektromagnetischen Wellen zu tun. Das heißt immer eine elektrische und eine magnetische Komponente. Weitere Optionen, die es theoretisch gibt und auch tatsächlich experimentell eingesetzt werden, ist die zirkulare Polarisation. Also wir sind auch in der Lage, dass sich die Welle oder der elektrische Feldvektor kreisförmig bewegt. In dem Fall, man könnte sagen, kurkenzieherartig auf uns zu gerät. Und in dem Fall gibt es kein Horizontal und kein Vertikal. Wir haben es ja mit einem Kreis zu tun. Was man hier unterscheiden würde, wäre die Drehrichtung. Ich kann also horizontal aussenden und dann die Antenne auf Vertikal empfangen umschalten. Das heißt, ich sende horizontal aus und empfange vertikal. Das heißt, über Kreuz. Horizontal aussenden, vertikal empfangen. Jetzt besteht natürlich die Frage, warum soll ich das tun? Tatsächlich ist bei dieser Kreuzpolarisation die Rückstreuintensität in der Regel sehr gering. Zumindest deutlich geringer als in den Q-Polarisationen, die sich ergeben würden, wenn ich horizontal aussende und horizontal empfange oder vertikal aussende und vertikal empfange. Dennoch gibt es viele Landoberflächen, die eine sehr hohe Kreuzpolarisation aufweisen können. Das passiert immer dann, wenn meine einfallende elektromagnetische Welle depolarisiert wird. Bei Volumenstreuungen erfolgt innerhalb dieses Streuvolumens die Streuung so oft, dass letzten Endes auch die Welle depolarisiert werden kann und am Ende ein gewisser Anteil auch vertikal polarisiert ist. Ein ganz typisches Beispiel dafür ist eben Vegetation. Also ein Anwendungsfall oder ein Beispiel wäre, dass wir im L-Band für Waldflächen eine sehr hohe HV-Komponente bekommen, während die HV-Komponente im L-Band für Flächen mit kurzer Vegetation, Feldvegetation oder relativ glatten Flächen oder vegetationsfreien Flächen sehr, sehr gering ist. Im Extremfall für Wasserflächen kann ich sogar ja theoretisch einen Wert von Null für HV messen. Das ist nur aus technischen Gesichtspunkten nicht möglich, da jeder Sensor auch ein gewisses Eigenrauschen, und das hat jetzt nichts mit Speckel zu tun, jeder Sensor ein gewisses Eigenrauschen mit sich bringt, durch die ganzen Stromflüsse im System selber quasi elektromagnetische Wellen generiert, die wiederum von der Empfangsantenne generiert werden. Das hat den ganz groben Zusammenhang, dass die Objekte, die mit unserer Radarwelle interagieren, ungefähr in der Größenordnung der Radarwelle selbst auch sind. Wenn wir uns das Beispiel eines Baumsmatorate ziehen wollen, ist es eben so, dass im X-Band, also im kurzwelligeren Bereich, auch die kleinen Objekte am Baum, sprich die Blätter, eine Rolle spielen und die Rückstreuung an den Blättern selbst erfolgt. Während für die großen Wellenlängen, P-Band beispielsweise um die 70 cm, die großen Bestandteile des Baumes, sprich der Stamm selbst und auch die großen Äste, die wesentlichen Objekte sind, die die Radarückstreuung generieren. Das lässt sich auch übertragen auf ein weiteres Beispiel, beispielsweise vegetationsfreie Landoberflächen. Nehmen wir mal unbestelltes Ackerland mit unterschiedlichen Rauigkeiten. Auch da ist es relevant, mit welcher Wellenlänge ich arbeite. Ein Feld kann beispielsweise für einen X-Band-Datensatz, also wirklich die kleine Wellenlänge, noch relativ rau erscheinen und für eine große Wellenlänge, L-Band oder P-Band, dafür schon ziemlich glatt erscheinen. Rau in dem Fall heißt, es wird eine höhere Rückstreuintensität generiert. Ein glattes Feld wird eher eine geringe Rückstreuintensität generieren. Wir sehen schon, Rauigkeit darf nicht unabhängig von der Wellenlänge betrachtet werden. Das Feld, das für die eine Wellenlänge schon glatt ist, ist für die andere Wellenlänge noch rau. Dafür gibt es auch ganz klare Kriterien, an denen das festgemacht werden kann. Ein zweiter wichtiger Aspekt, den wir besprechen müssen, ist, dass unterschiedliche Wellenlängen auch zu unterschiedlichen Eindringtiefen in unterschiedliche Objekte führen können. Beispielsweise ist man mit langwelligen Daten, also L- oder P-Band, viel besser in der Lage, tiefer in ein Kronendach einzudringen. Das P-Band beispielsweise wird es schaffen, bis zum Waldboden vorzudringen und dort zurückgestreut zu werden, während ein X-Band-Sensor tatsächlich fast ausschließlich die Oberfläche des Kronendachs erfasst.
