Pourquoi utiliser le SAR ? Pourquoi utiliser le SAR ? Pourquoi utiliser le SAR ? Le radar d'ouverture synthétique, communément appelé SAR, est un instrument actif qui opère à des fréquences de micro-ondes. Il peut imaginer la surface de l'océan pendant la nuit et le jour et n'est pas affecté par le couvre-cloud. Cette capacité à offrir une situation maritime sous n'importe quelle circonstance est un avantage clé comparé à l'imagerie optique. La haute résolution et la grande quantité d'imagerie de SAR, font qu'il est un outil unique pour détecter précisément et mapper les déchets d'huile et les bateaux sur de grandes zones maritimes. Les systèmes de radar opèrent en L-band, ce qui est bon pour la détection des ondes, par exemple, ou en X-band, ce qui est bon pour obtenir une haute résolution, pour la détection de bateaux. Généralement, pour les activités de détection de déchets d'huile, nous utilisons des radars C-band, comme le Sentinel-1 européen ou le SAT-2 canadien, ce qui est un bon compromis pour toutes les applications maritimes. Alors, comment fonctionne-t-il ? L'instrument SAR mesure l'intensité du signal qui est écarté de la surface de l'océan et utilise l'histoire Doppler pour synthétiser la haute résolution dans la direction de la route. Lorsque l'on imagine la surface de l'océan, le signal écarté de la surface de l'océan contient des informations sur le niveau de rougessie de la surface de l'océan, qui est principalement conduit par la vitesse de vent locale et la direction par rapport à la ligne de vue de l'antenne de radar. Généralement, l'intensité du signal écarté de la surface de l'océan augmente avec la vitesse de vent. L'instrument SAR possède une unique capacité de capturer un grand panneau de phénomènes à large échelle, tels que l'huile, les vagues, la France, les cellules de pluie, etc. Pas directement, mais la façon dont ces phénomènes à large échelle contribuent à moduler la rougessie de la surface de l'océan, qui est actuellement vu par l'instrument de radar. Alors, comment l'image SAR écarte l'huile ? Nous avons juste vu que l'instrument SAR est sensitif à la rougessie de la surface de l'océan, plus précisément à des vagues centimétriques générées par le vent, parfois appelées des vagues Bragg, dans un mécanisme de rougessie de la surface de l'océan. Comme l'huile est une matière viscose, quand il y a un déchet d'huile, les vagues centimétriques de la surface sont déchirées, et le signal écarté de l'océan qui est retourné à l'instrument SAR est diminué, ce qui résulte en zones plus sombres sur les images SAR. content: Les signatures SAR des déchets d'huile peuvent avoir un nombre d'aspects sur les images de SAR, en fonction de leur âge, en fonction des conditions de l'état de la mer, en fonction de la configuration d'observation. Elles peuvent être affectées par la fréquence de radar, par la polarisation, par l'angle d'incidence, mais en gros, la vitesse de vent est le facteur le plus limitant. Alors, comment les conditions de vent influencent la façon dont les SAR imagent les déchets d'huile, en particulier dans le cas de Sibban, qui est le rang typique de la SAR que nous utilisons pour la détection des déchets d'huile. En cas de faible vent, disons en dessous de 2 ou 3 mètres par seconde, le contraste entre les zones polluées d'huile et l'eau propre peut être très faible, ce qui rend la détection des déchets d'huile très difficile. Et de telles conditions de faible vent sont aussi favorables à la génération de films naturels qui ont une nature SAR très similaire à l'huile et qui peut conduire à une misinterprétation. Les vents modérés, qui sont de 3 à 10 à 12 mètres par seconde, sont le rang typique de la vitesse de vent qui permet une bonne détection, en général, de détection d'huile. Mais à hauts vents, au-dessus de 12 à 15 mètres par seconde, la détection d'huile est limitée par des turbulences et des vagues qui dispersent l'huile dans la colonne d'eau. Alors, comment fonctionne une service de détection des déchets d'huile ? En fait, la partie la plus compliquée d'un service de détection des déchets d'huile consiste à distinguer des déchets d'huile réels avec des ressemblances. Il y a plusieurs phénomènes naturels dans l'océan ouvert qui ont une nature SAR qui peut être interprétée comme de l'huile et reportée erroneusement comme tel. Nous les appelons des alarmes fausses. Les alarmes fausses peuvent arriver d'un nombre de situations. Par exemple, l'interaction de courants de vagues entre deux masses d'eau qui génèrent des zones de convergence qui résultent d'une diminution de la rougesse de la surface de l'océan et qui peut être interprétée comme de l'huile. Les alarmes fausses peuvent aussi arriver, par exemple, de l'insertion de l'eau froide dans un système plus chaud qui peut aussi conduire à une zone plus sombre dans l'image SAR et qui peut être méprisée comme l'huile. Il y a souvent des conditions de faible vent qui sont rencontrées dans les îles de Lille, dans les montagnes de Lille, et cela peut aussi être confus avec l'image SAR de l'huile. Donc, il y a un nombre de situations, nous pouvons aussi mentionner les zones de convergence, les thèmes naturels, toutes ces situations qui sont très confuses. Pour résoudre toutes ces situations ambigües, l'expérience de l'analyste qui supervise le service de détection d'huile est essentielle. Je dirais même que c'est probablement l'une des parties les plus importantes du service de détection d'huile. La condition de temps commune, maintenant établie par l'entreprise EMSA Clean Cnet Service, est un délai de 30 minutes entre l'acquisition de l'image SAR et la délivraison du rapport d'huile. Ce délai peut même être réduit à 20 minutes, quand l'huile est en cours pendant le temps d'acquisition de l'image SAR. Réduire ce délai augmente les chances d'attraper le vaisseau polluant à la main rouge. Mais un délai si court ne peut être atteint qu'après l'acquisition, si l'image SAR est déconnectée de la station de terrain la plus proche. La chaîne de service consiste à trois étapes principales de la procédure. La première étape, la télémétrie SAR est déconnectée de la station de terrain, puis processée de niveau 0 à niveau 1 pour obtenir l'image SAR. Ensuite, jusqu'à les produits de niveau 2, des produits de valeur ajoutés, comme une carte de vaisseaux détectés, une carte d'huile mesurée de l'image SAR et une carte de déchets. Cela prend environ 5 à 10 minutes. Ensuite, l'image SAR est analysée par un opérateur bien traîné. Tous les déchets ou déchets d'huile potentiels détectés sont vérifiés, qualifiés et confirmés par l'analyste. Si il y a une pollution d'huile, l'analyste essaie même d'identifier la source potentielle de la pollution en utilisant des informations ancillaires comme l'AIS, le système d'identification automatique, ou un modèle de déchets d'huile. Cela prend environ 10 à 20 minutes. Enfin, toute cette information est compilée dans un rapport de détection d'huile de déchets d'huile contenant des informations sur l'huile, les bateaux, les vents, les vagues, même les paramètres de qualité. Ce rapport de détection d'huile de déchets d'huile est envoyé aux utilisateurs finaux au cours des 5 dernières minutes. Le service CleanSeaNet a été en opération depuis 2007, avec plus de 2 500 images SAR analysées par jour. Cela a clairement démontré son effet déterrent sur les bateaux polluants. Au cours de cette période, le nombre de déchets d'huile détectés par km2 a été divisé en trois par rapport aux eaux européennes. Mais il y a maintenant beaucoup d'autres applications pour la surveillance maritime qui sont fournies dans le cadre de la sécurité maritime de Copernicus. Par exemple, la détection d'activités de pêche illégale qui s'adresse à la détection des bateaux illégaux dans des zones restrictives, comme les zones économiques exclusives. Les images SAR sont aussi utilisées pour surveiller les frontières maritimes, pour soutenir la détection de petits bateaux remplis de réfugiés dans la mer Méditerranéenne, par exemple. Les images SAR sont aussi utilisées pour mieux comprendre et monitoriser les crimes environnementaux, tels que la logistique illégale et le trafic associé par les voies maritimes.

Ces détails ne sont pas capturés par le modèle atmosphérique océanique, mais ils peuvent être vus clairement dans les vents SAAR. Si j'affiche la signature du vent sur la surface, c'est en fait une augmentation de la rougesse de la surface de la mer. C'est ce que nous voyons dans l'image SAAR. La couche arrière devient plus brillante, et nous voyons même des endroits beaucoup plus brillants. Et ces endroits plus brillants sont en fait l'impact de la pluie sur la surface de la mer.

content: Je m'appelle Bertrand Chaperon et je travaille à l'IFROMER, l'institut français pour l'océanographie et la recherche. En parlant aujourd'hui du mécanisme de scattering de la surface océanique, nous devons rappeler que le radar est très sensitif à la rougesseur de courte échelle sur une surface. Pour la surface océanique, la petite échelle signifie que nous commençons par des ondes mimétriques, des ondes capillaires, entourant les ondes capillaires de gravité d'un certain nombre de centimètres jusqu'à les ondes les plus grosses, les ondes d'échelle de quelques centimètres. Avec le radar, nous sommes en mesure de détecter la courte échelle, et grâce à cette détection, nous pouvons définir de nombreuses applications. Pour mieux comprendre le mécanisme de scattering, il faut bien comprendre le fait que lorsque la pluie brûle sur la surface, la petite échelle va grandir sous la puissance de cette pluie. La petite échelle va aussi grandir directionnellement en fonction de la direction de la pluie. Ainsi, l'intensité du radar va détecter la puissance des ondes de courte échelle autour de la pluie, et dépendra également de la direction de la pluie. Donc, pour commencer, nous devons rappeler que la rougesseur, dominée par la pluie locale, va gouverner la puissance du signal de radar. Maintenant, lorsque nous considérons un instrument d'imagination de radar, nous devons considérer que cet instrument peut opérer à différents angles d'incidence, avec différents états de polarisation, ainsi qu'en utilisant différentes longues vagues. En fonction de cette longue vague, ou en fonction de la polarisation, vous ne détecterez pas clairement le même type de rougesseur. La puissance du signal de radar va être modulée en fonction de cette puissance. La puissance du signal de radar, dominée par la pluie locale, et par la direction de la pluie locale, va ensuite changer en fonction du changement de la rougesseur. La rougesseur est très sensitive à la tension, à la viscosité, ce qui signifie qu'un petit changement de la rougesseur sera détecté comme un petit changement de la puissance du signal de radar. Sur l'océan, si la surface est plus chaude, ou si la surface est calme et plus froide, vous obtiendrez différents modèles de radar. C'est ce que nous utilisons pour définir et rétablir l'algorithme pour interpréter l'image de radar. Le radar est un instrument très, très sensible à la géométrie. En fonction de l'angle d'incidence, vous obtiendrez plus de retour de radar pour un angle d'incidence plus bas, et un angle d'incidence plus petit pour un angle d'incidence plus grand. En même temps, lorsque vous avez une polarisation verticale, vous obtiendrez un signal de radar plus puissant en comparaison avec un signal de polarisation horizontale. Et maintenant, la surface apportera également un signal cross-polarisé qui sera très, très bas en comparaison avec les signaux copoles, mais qui sont toujours utilisés pour déterminer la puissance de la vitesse de vent. Pour continuer à mieux comprendre l'algorithme de radar sur l'océan, nous savons que la surface locale exhibera un tilt local. Par conséquent, le plomb, par exemple, modulera le signal de radar parce que la vague qui arrive au radar ou qui s'éloigne du radar n'aura pas la même échelle et nous aidera ainsi à imaginer les vagues à travers le changement du tilt des vagues longues. Les vagues courtes dominent les signaux de backscatter minimes, tandis que les vagues plus longues moduleront ce signal de radar minime pour fournir l'image des vagues sur la surface de l'océan. De même, si, par exemple, vous avez un changement dans la tension de la surface à cause du film biologique ou des polluants, les vagues courtes seront éloignées. Ainsi, les vagues courtes disparaissent, votre puissance de signal du radar disparaîtra également. L'image du radar aura probablement l'air très sombre en comparaison avec les signaux de retour de l'océan à l'arrière. Cela aide à distinguer l'endroit où il y a la pollution ainsi que l'endroit où il y a des effets de divergence de courant de surface. Au-dessus de ce mécanisme de backscatter, vous savez que la rougesse de la surface de l'océan qui s'accumule sous l'action de la pluie, brûle aussi, car la façon de dissiper l'énergie de la pluie vers l'océan est de produire des vagues qui brûlent. Les vagues qui brûlent auront différentes signatures dans le signal du radar. Généralement, la polarisation est perdue quand il y a des vagues qui brûlent. Les signals de radar copoles, verticaux et horizontaux seront plus proches, ce qui signifie que la polarisation sera minimisée en présence des vagues qui brûlent. Les vagues qui brûlent s'accumulent naturellement sur l'océan, mais s'accumuleront plus probablement sur un gradient de surface puissant où vous aurez une convergence de courant de surface. C'est aussi une façon de moduler le signal du radar et de détecter cet événement et de fournir des informations sur l'occurrence du gradient de courant. Nous verrons aussi que, en utilisant un radar, vous avez aussi la capacité de mesurer un changement dans la fréquence Doppler associée au courant de surface ou à la motion des vagues de surface. En effet, pas seulement les vagues de surface de l'océan changent localement la géométrie de l'observation, elles aussi changent la kinématique. Ainsi, en utilisant un radar, vous mesurez à la fois l'intensité du radar, mais aussi le changement du Doppler en raison de la présence de vagues qui propagent sur l'océan. Le Doppler, ainsi que le signal du radar, sont aussi une fonction de la polarisation, aussi une fonction de la longueur de courant, ainsi que de l'angle d'incidence. Ces motions sont aussi probables d'être associées à la direction du vent, telles que la propagation des vagues à vous, ou la propagation des vagues contre vous, n'auront pas le même Doppler. Le Doppler va changer de signe. Pour continuer l'analyse du signal du radar sur l'océan, nous devons rappeler que nous devons comprendre la distribution de la rougesse, le changement de la distribution de la rougesse en raison du tilt local des vagues, et le changement du Doppler en raison de la motion orbitale des vagues. Savoir tous ces détails aidera à interpréter la plupart des images du radar que nous obtenons quotidiennement à partir de mesures satellites. La résolution que nous obtenons aujourd'hui est de l'ordre de 10 mètres, ou mieux, et grâce à cette capacité d'imagination, nous pouvons résoudre localement la direction du vent et la puissance de l'océan, la direction des vagues et la longueur des vagues, ainsi que la présence d'un courant sur la surface de l'océan. Dans le futur, nous pourrons utiliser cette information avec d'autres instruments, en combinant toutes ces informations pour offrir une meilleure application pour les vagues et les courants.

content: The synthetic aperture radar, short name the SAR, has a fantastic capability to detect the surface roughness at the ocean surface with very high spatial resolution. This allows us to take out the contributor to the surface roughness which is among those most dominating the surface wind. Wind at the ocean surface has two properties. It has the speed, the wind speed, the strength and it has a direction and the synthetic aperture radar is in fact able to detect the directional properties of this in one image. Meaning that if the wind blows towards the radar antenna it has a very strong return signal. If the wind is blowing across the radar antenna or the radar loop direction, the sensitivity is much weaker and this is both a valuable knowledge for us but at the same time it's a challenge for us. If we do not know anything about the background wind speed and direction we may fool ourself into the wrong estimate. Now if we are near land and we can use a little bit of the land in the image then this helps a lot. We can more or less immediately know take out the wind direction because of the signal in the near shore, the path. Whereas in the open ocean we need to maybe know a little bit about the large-scale weather conditions then we have immediately an indication of the direction, the large-scale direction and we know it and we can go in and we can take out the radar cross-section and basically relate it to the wind speed. And up to now we've been able to detect wind speed in the range from a few meters per second up all the way to above 30 meters per second which is hurricane winds and with great details in terms of spatial resolution of let's say hundreds of meters we can say something about the fine dynamic characteristics associated with low-pressure systems which has not been possible to observe with general observing system because of its lack of resolution. Today we see that the use of the SAR for detecting winds is a sort of a by-product. If we can remove the wind from the ocean surface then we are immediately in a better position to take out the rest of the roughness on the ocean surface and associate that with waves and with currents and this is exactly what we do. Waves on the ocean surface has another characteristic wavelength. It is typically waves in the order of hundred meters and they will be quite the structure so there's patterns of waves as you've been in the ocean you know that and this pattern is immediately detected in the SAR image because of the fine spatial resolution and we have very good ability to immediately claim that this is ocean surface waves nothing else. So in that type of observations we can characterize the wavelength, we can characterize the amplitude and out of that we can estimate the spectrum which is what is usually the drive in ocean wave modeling. You sort of simulate the wave spectrum and you predict the changes in the spectrum forward in time. So now we observe this with the SAR and we combine it with the wave models and all together we have a better initial position to sort of give a more reliable forecast in the next state of the ocean and the surface roughness characteristics. So wave observations is then another quite distinct type of applications of SAR data and it has demonstrated its ability to be highly important for monitoring waves in the ocean surface and we see fascinating signals where waves generated in the southern hemisphere by low-pressure systems coming into the southern ocean travels all the way across the Pacific Ocean cross equator and reach the shores in Alaska in North Pacific. It takes them about 10-15 days to do that travel but we observe it with the SAR data. Absolutely a fascinating way to monitor waves on the ocean surface. Now moving on then we have been able to know the roughness associated with winds and associated with waves. We can also then in a way remove that contribution to the roughness signal and the remaining part now shall be the surface current. This is a very delicate situation where we are still sort of challenged by all the details that can be occurring in terms of the mixed contribution of wind waves and current but the more we can be sure that we take out the wind and the wave contribution the more we are confident that what we are left with are the surface current signals. Predominantly today we can do this in two ways. Surface current boundaries are extremely important to monitor. It is along the surface current boundaries that all the vertical motions is most dominant. This is where things are being accumulated or this is where things are being pushed down or coming up. So it has a rich relationship with biology. Boundaries of currents seen in SAR images is again manifested through a very detailed and confined surface roughness anomalies. This is wave current interaction in a very gentle play but the SAR detects it and we are confident that we are able to also take it out of the SAR images. So we can align these fronts to be characteristic of the boundaries of the strong currents. Recently also we have been able to do another thing which is a direct retrieval of the surface velocity of the ocean surface and that's taking into account the Doppler principle. In order to understand the Doppler principle one have to be a little bit confident with the principle of the SAR because it is a measure of amplitude and phase and if you are only measuring amplitude you would not be able to do this. But thanks to the fact that is also measuring the phase of the signals we can look at phase shifts and in the phase shifts we are able to reconstruct the total motion of the surface. And now if we again know the wind, the wind direction and the wind speed, we know the wave propagation direction, we can take out those contributors to the phase shift and what we are left with is the phase shift induced by the surface surface current. So this is shown now to be feasible with the SAR systems as well and it is a very important additional new contribution to the ocean observations with SAR.

content: Maintenant, je vais vous montrer la propagation de la vague dans l'eau de la mer que nous pouvons voir du radar d'ouverture synthétique. C'est la vue de l'océan arctique. Vous avez la concentration de l'eau dans le fond, que vous voyez en blanc et bleu quand la concentration s'approche de zéro. Cela vous donne une idée de l'étage de l'eau à basse résolution. Si vous commencez à zoomer, vous voyez que la vague a un signal assez distinct sur l'eau de la mer. Nous voyons clairement l'étage de l'eau de la mer et si vous regardez encore plus proche, vous commencez à voir ce pattern de vague entrer dans l'eau de la mer et disparaître à un moment ou l'eau de la mer commence à devenir trop rigide. C'est donc une indication de la zone d'eau marginale, qui est l'endroit où les vagues sont capables de voyager dans l'eau de la mer. C'est la définition de la zone d'eau marginale. Vous pouvez voir une pénétration assez différente des vagues dans la zone d'eau marginale en fonction du type d'eau. Dans certaines zones, la distance est très courte, l'atténuation est très rapide. Dans d'autres zones, vous pouvez voir des propagations de vagues dans l'eau de l'océan sur des centaines de kilomètres. Ceci n'est pas utilisé personnellement, mais devrait vous donner l'indication de la capacité de naviguer dans l'eau de l'océan. C'est une des applications émergentes et évoluantes du radar de capteur synthétique dans l'Arctique. Il s'agit de pouvoir identifier l'endroit où la navigation sera possible ou non. Ici, vous voyez clairement qu'avec ce polygone, j'illumine la présence de vagues dans l'eau de l'océan, qu'elle n'est pas bien distribuée avec la distance de l'étage de l'océan. C'est vraiment dépendant de la durabilité et probablement de la profondeur de l'eau de l'océan. C'est quelque chose que nous examinerons dans le futur pour développer plus d'algorithmes pour automatiquement détecter les vagues qui atteignent les régions polaires dans l'eau de l'océan.

content: So, again, thanks to the fact that the SAR is sensing the surface roughness, it is also used quite a lot for monitoring sea ice in the high latitude waters, both in the Northern Hemisphere and in the Southern Hemisphere. And detecting sea ice is in itself extremely important. Along the ice edge, there are fascinating processes that lead to a very strong biological activity, which is still not fully understood. Even during winter, in the presence of no light, there are significant amounts of observations of rich biology activity. So the ice edge is really a place where there are bio-optical conditions in the water that really favours rich ecosystems. And therefore, to find these ice edges continuously is done regularly from satellites. The Synthetic Aperture Radar Satellites, again, because it is having such a fantastic resolution, gives us the possibility to detect individual sea ice flows, to track their motion, which is not just a straight line, they usually rotate around due to tidal motions and inertial motions. And the more we can observe this, and the more we can frequently observe this, the more we have an ability to not just take out the motion, but also explain the contributors to the total motion. The SAR is an enormously important contributor to this. And also keep in mind that if you want to navigate in ice-covered seas, you need to know a little bit about where is it easy to go and where is it complicated to go. The SAR is the only sensing system from satellite that can do that. And we see over and over how it is practised these days, where the ice-breaking research vessels, when they go into the Arctic Ocean, they use continuous information from the SAR to find the easy way to go. So in future, you can imagine if we will see ship rooting from Europe to Asia during summertime because of little ice in the Arctic Ocean, again, this system will be highly critical in order to make safely opportunities to undertake this kind of operation.

content: Ok, maintenant nous allons voir comment les courants sur la surface de l'océan peuvent être vus par un radar d'ouverture synthétique, une démonstration avec Sentinel-1. Je vais donc d'abord sélectionner les données de Sentinel-1, et nous allons regarder dans une zone où il s'agit d'une courant très forte, la courant d'Aguilas, en Afrique du Sud. Lorsque nous zoomons, nous pouvons voir sur l'image de la courant d'Aguilas une grossesse plus élevée dans une zone où la courant de la surface est en fait face aux ondes, ce qui introduit plus de grossesse. Nous voyons donc l'arrière plus brillante de la courant d'Aguilas. Et si nous éloignons le changement de Doppler, le changement de Doppler est la vitesse vers le radar, et nous voyons également qu'à la frontière de la courant, il y a un changement de vitesse fort vers le radar. Donc ce changement de Doppler n'est pas encore calibré, mais nous pouvons déjà voir la motion relative à la courant de la surface. Nous pouvons également appliquer un modèle d'une courant d'océan. C'est un modèle d'OCEANIC qui prévoit la courant d'océan. Ici nous voyons les lignes d'eau de la courant d'océan. Nous voyons clairement qu'il y a un accord avec la location que nous voyons sur l'image de la courant d'océan, mais en même temps, la frontière de la courant d'océan n'est pas aussi claire que ce que nous voyons sur l'observation. Nous pouvons également appliquer une température sur la surface de l'océan, en retirant l'outil modèle et en ajoutant un peu de transparence. Nous pouvons donc voir que la frontière de la courant d'océan est à la même location que le changement de température sur la surface de l'océan. C'est clairement une courant chaude qui passe du nord-ouest au sud-ouest de la côte africaine du Sud. Nous avons aussi la possibilité d'appliquer les trajectoires de la courant d'océan. Les trajectoires de la courant d'océan sont en fait des bouilles flottantes, qui ont une longueur de 15 mètres sous la surface et qui flottent avec la courant d'océan. Nous représentons la trajectoire de la courant d'océan pendant un mois, et la couleur est proportionnelle à la vitesse. Comme nous pouvons le voir, la vitesse va de 0 à 2,5 mètres par seconde. Et dans l'arrière de la courant d'océan, nous pouvons atteindre 2 mètres par seconde. Nous avons donc une consistance entre ce que nous voyons sur l'image de la courant d'océan et la trajectoire de la courant d'océan.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Water Body Mapping with Sentinel-1

content: Here we have a fantastic view of the impressive Forth Rail and Road bridges crossing a mighty water body which is the Forth River estuary, otherwise known as the Firth of Forth in Scotland. A water body is any significant accumulation of water from oceans to small ponds. It may contain salt water, brackish water or fresh water. It also includes wetlands. Wetlands are transition zones from dry to permanently wet ecosystems and comprise such environments as peatlands, bogs, wet meadows, floodplains, floodplain forests and reed beds. Wetlands include flora and fauna habitats which are adapted to unique conditions and the monitoring of wetlands is essential to ensure preservation of biodiversity. The monitoring of wetlands is also important given their multiple functions in the carbon cycle. They are a source of methane and peatlands act as carbon dioxide sinks. Floods are also temporary water bodies which occur when water submerges usually dry land. Floods often take place along rivers, lakes, seashores or in flat areas which may become saturated with water such as after heavy rain. Floods cause physical damage and affect water, food and crop supplies and may contribute to the spread of waterborne diseases. Inland water bodies in high latitudes provide us with an indicator of climate change and changes in their size are linked to permafrost degradation. Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music Music SAR remote sensing is particularly suitable for the mapping of water surfaces given that it is based on often relatively simple differences in the backscatter regimes of water and land surfaces. Calm water surfaces are smooth and cause specular reflection leading to low backscatter. Surrounding land surfaces are rougher by comparison and lead to higher backscatter. Challenges in SAR mapping of water bodies occur in vegetated areas with vegetation emerging from the water increasing the surface roughness and therefore also the backscatter. Long wavelengths are preferable in these cases due to better penetration of vegetation cover. Another challenge can occur if there are trees, buildings or other large vertical structures emerging from water bodies. The presence of smooth right angled corners in such areas can produce strong double bounce scattering and enhance the backscatter of the otherwise smooth and therefore low backscattering water surface. Higher backscatter may also be present where there are wet soils not completely submerged by water. These produce higher backscatter than drier soils due to their increased relative permittivity or dielectric constant. A further difficulty in mapping water bodies may be encountered if there are wind or current driven waves on the water surface. Particularly when these propagate in an orientation perpendicular to the direction of flight they can increase the roughness of the water surface and produce stronger backscatter. One simple and common method for water body mapping is thresholding. The backscatter below a threshold is classified as a water body, the backscatter above a threshold is classified as dry land. These thresholds can be derived from image histograms. The contrast between the backscatter of land and open water surfaces increases with increasing incidence angle. If a choice of polarisation is available HH is more suitable for wetland detection given that it is less affected by vertical vegetation structures and VV is more sensitive to soil moisture and flood conditions. The crosspole component such as HV or VH provides a good discrimination of woody versus herbaceous vegetation types due to its sensitivity to biomass. Other parts of the Firth have seen significant changes to their extents. For example as a result of land reclamation for industry and agriculture the inner Firth beyond these bridges and as far as the town of Kincardine has lost about half of its former intertidal area. Regular monitoring of this and other water bodies is therefore of crucial importance.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space - Water: Water Body Mapping

content: Marconi wasn't just interested in transmitting radio signals across the Atlantic. He was also interested in how you could use these radio signals for many practical applications beyond just radio communications. And in 1922, he made a presentation to the American Institute of Electrical Engineers to explain and describe quite a detailed system that we would now call radar. It involved transmitting radio waves and determining not just the distance to the target but also giving you an indication of roughly which direction it was in. Now, at this point, there was much interest in developing these systems but it started to go more into the military intelligence and mapping communities so that many of the experiments from around about the 1920s and 30s onwards were all conducted in secret. Many of the experiments that followed Marconi's concept were done, for example, by the US Navy Research Labs.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: 1st Radar Concept

content: Radar in space didn't happen until the 1970s. The Skylab mission had a small radio altimeter, and that was used to demonstrate in principle that you could use radar systems in space, but it wasn't an imaging system. The first imaging system in space was the CSAT satellite, launched in June 1978. CSAT, as its name suggests, was optimised for looking at the ocean surface, and this was an L-band imaging radar system. Now even though the system failed after about four months, the amount of data and new data that was collected was so different from what had been looked at before in the Earth observation community, that in fact for many years afterwards people were still analysing and exploring and understanding the data that the CSAT mission had collected.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: 1st Satellite

content: By 1940 all of the military radar systems had been ground-based. This was partly a consequence of the fact that they needed to generate large amounts of power and also they needed large antennas. This meant that they were transmitting very long wavelengths, many tens of meters. The next advance was how do you get one of these radar systems onto an aircraft. If you have an antenna larger than about 1.5 meters you wouldn't be able to fit it onto the aircraft. What it needed was the development of something that could generate small wavelengths, so you didn't need such a large antenna, and lots of power. And in 1940 the British invented the cavity magnetron. This was the first system that actually generated short wavelengths, so about 10 centimeter wavelengths, in a consistent high-energy fashion. This allowed them to take radar systems and actually put them into aircraft. As a consequence of that the first airborne radar systems were born. The H2S system by the British went on bombers and was actually used to map the ground surface through cloud cover and at night. It is one of the unfortunate things about radar remote sensing, that we cannot separate ourselves from a history that involves military instrumentation and development, mostly in secret and largely used in the context of wartime.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: 1st airborne radar

content: Following on from the development of airborne radar systems during World War II, the military in many countries continued to develop improved systems of radar systems on aircraft looking at the ground. Carl Wiley in 1952 at the Goodyear Aircraft Corporation developed what we now consider to be Doppler beam sharpening. This was one of the key developments in being able to improve the spatial resolution of radar systems even with small antennas. Now much of this work was being conducted in secret but in 1967 there was the first civilian application of airborne radar. The Darien province in Panama was mapped by an airborne radar system because this area had been so covered in cloud that in fact none of the airborne surveys had been able to properly map all the rivers and all the mountains going into this area of Panama. This was a key development in airborne radar because it was now into the civilian domain and everybody could see the key advantages that you could get from having a radar system on an aircraft to map the earth's surface.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: 1st civilian airborne

content: In the 1930s there was a key scientific interest in using range finding with radio waves. This was in a meteorological context looking to see if you could detect not just the location of impending storm clouds but also their direction. There was a group in the United Kingdom led by Edward Appleton that included people such as Robert Watson Watt who were involved in looking at pulsed radar systems to transmit a radio signal up into the atmosphere and to detect the echoes coming back. As well as determining that they could see large storm clouds at a distance, they also discovered that you could bounce signals off a layer in the atmosphere that we know as the ionosphere. And in fact one of those layers is called the Appleton layer in recognition of Edward Appleton's work on this subject.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Direction & Range

content: The European Space Agency decided to launch a seabed system in 1991. The seabed system was called ERS-1 for Earth Remote Sensing Satellite. Seabed was chosen as the best wavelength for oceanographic applications. In the 80s, it was mostly believed that radar mainly will be applied for oceanographic monitoring. But when ERS-1 was launched, it became obvious that due to the operational monitoring of land surfaces, also land applications should be developed. Since originally ERS-1 was only manufactured for a three-year lifetime, in 1995 ERS-2, the second Earth Remote Sensing Satellite, was launched by the European Space Agency. ERS-1, however, lived on for almost a decade. So two identical systems were in space that could be used for interferometric applications on a repeat path mode. This history led to a third seabed deployment on the Envisat satellite bus called the ASAR system, which continued a seabed timeline from 1991, starting with ERS-1, until 2010.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: ERS 1

content: Michael Faraday was one of the most exciting experimental scientists of the 19th century. He conducted many important experiments in the basement of the Royal Society in London during the first half of the 19th century. In 1845 he made a particularly important discovery, which was that if he applied a magnetic field across a medium while he passed a light beam through it, he could influence the properties of the light beam with the magnetic field. This was significant because it was the first demonstration that electricity and magnetism were related. Up until then they had been seen as entirely different phenomena. It was this experimental result that made the groundwork that allowed James Clerk Maxwell to develop the overarching theory of electromagnetic radiation.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Faraday

content: How does radar remote sensing continue? Already in the pipeline is the NASA system, NISAR. Also, already in the pipeline is a very exciting Earth Explorer mission designed by the European Space Agency. It's called Biomass. This is a P-band system. P-band uses 70 cm wavelengths. It's specifically designed to map the above-ground carbon stored in our tropical forests, for which we need very long radar wavelengths to penetrate this forest canopy. Further countries are in the process of launching radar satellites such as India, China, Argentina, and many others. The European Copernicus Program has already decided for the upcoming decades to continue their series of sentinels. So already in the planning are Sentinel-C and D, Sentinel-1C and D, so to continue the C-band time series for the decades to come.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Future Missions

content: A great place to start with the history of radar is around about 1800. There was a lot of excitement around about that time about electricity. Scientists such as Volta and Galvani had been looking at electricity and how not only could you control it in the laboratory, but you could actually apply it to animal tissue. Galvani conducted a famous experiment where he applied electricity to a dead frog and found that when he applied the electricity to the nerves of the frog, he could make the legs twitch. This was an exciting time where the Leyden jar had been invented so you could actually store electricity and you could start to do experiments in the lab.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Galvani

content: It's fair to say that James Clerk Maxwell's work of 1865 was so groundbreaking and written in a way which was quite impenetrable that it took a long time before the scientific community was able to both understand and to test the theories that Maxwell had put forward. In 1886 Heinrich Hertz actually did some laboratory experiments with a small kit that generated some electricity by putting a spark across two copper wires and by doing so was able to transfer a radio wave a small distance across his lab. This electromagnetic wave, as predicted by James Clerk Maxwell's theories, did all the same things that you would expect a wave to do. He was able to reflect it, he was able to refract it through objects, he was able to do interference and he could see the peaks and troughs of the interference patterns that he generated with these new waves. As a result, Hertz was able to demonstrate that the electromagnetic wave theory was indeed correct. Hertz's name is still used today in the units of frequency. The units of per second are named after Heinrich Hertz. This is a mock-up of the actual experiment that Heinrich Hertz conducted in 1886 to demonstrate that James Clerk Maxwell's theory was correct. So the induction coil generates a voltage across these two points here in these copper wires and when it generates a spark there's a current through the copper wires that generates an electromagnetic wave. Now the actual experiment he would have done, the wires were maybe twice as long, but what he was able to do is to generate waves of about a metre long in wavelength in the laboratory and fire across different parts of the laboratory to test to see if it acted like a wave. And indeed he discovered that the waves were polarised, that you could measure peaks and troughs, that you could interfere two different waves, that you could reflect them and that they obeyed Snell's law, that you could refract them and diffract them round edges. And it was this experiment that conclusively showed that James Clerk Maxwell's theory of electromagnetic waves was correct.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Hertz

content: In 1993, Didier Massonet and his co-authors published a remarkable piece of work that showed that you could do interferometry from space. Interferometry is when you're actually measuring the phase of the wave, so what stage the wave cycle is at, and that determines very, very small changes in distance that allow you to look at the Earth's surface and how it moves on a scale of a few centimetres. Their work published in Nature showed that the consequences of an earthquake and the small ground displacements could actually be measured from space.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Interferometry

content: Hi, my name's Ian Woodhouse. I'm a Professor of Applied Earth Observation at the University of Edinburgh and I'm an expert in radar remote sensing. If you want to learn about radar remote sensing, one of the things you have to realise is that the history of radar remote sensing is very different from everything you've learnt about optical and visible remote sensing. If you take an object like a mobile phone, there's a camera in the mobile phone and the history of that camera as a remote sensing device goes back to the 19th century and the invention of photography and then colour photography and then infrared photography and then digital scanners. And that history took those instruments and put them onto balloons and aircraft. But there's another remote sensing device in this smartphone and that's the ability to detect radio waves or microwaves. And the history of microwave remote sensing, which is vital to understanding how radars work, goes back to the early part of the 19th century and understanding that the history of radar had almost no influence whatsoever of the history of optical and camera and photography development.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Introduction

content: I'm currently sitting in the dining room of James Clark Maxwell's family home in Edinburgh. This was the house that he was born in, in 14 India Street. James Clark Maxwell is significant for the history of radar remote sensing because in 1865 he published his work on the theory of electromagnetic waves. This was extremely significant. It brought together all of the experimental results of the first half of the 19th century and brought it into a theory that was overarching and described all of the phenomena that had been seen to date. One of the key things and results from his theoretical analysis was that he could predict the speed of these waves. And I'll read to you what he said in his paper. He said, this velocity is so nearly that of light that it seems we have strong reason to conclude that light itself, including radiant heat and other radiations if any, is an electromagnetic disturbance in the form of waves. So James Clark Maxwell's paper brought together all the experimental work on electricity and magnetism and light and demonstrated that they could all be described with a small set of formula. So they were all the same phenomena, but just under different conditions. For electromagnetic waves, this was variations in frequency or wavelength, but all with the same velocity. So for the first time there was a general theory that described all of the properties of electromagnetic radiation, from the radio waves that the likes of Faraday had been experimenting with in the laboratory, to the light waves that people like Young and Fresnel had been experimenting on. And it also included the infrared and the thermal radiation and the other radiation like ultraviolet that had also been explored beyond the visible part of the spectrum. This is a significant point in the history of radar remote sensing.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Maxwell

content: After the end of the Second World War, there were many radio and radar engineers that were no longer required. Many of them went off to universities or research institutes and continued much of the work that they did, but outwards towards the galaxies. In 1961, for example, some radar engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory were able to transmit a signal from Earth and bounce it off of Venus. This gave extremely accurate measures of the distance from Earth to Venus. As a consequence, you can then make much more accurate measurements of the distance between Earth and the Sun. If you know accurate measurements of the Earth to the Sun distance, then when you're looking at the nearby stars in our own galaxy, and you're using the principle of parallax, so essentially stereo pictures of the nearby stars, is if you know the baseline of your stereo picture extremely accurately, you can make much more accurate measurements of how far away those stars are. So these early radar measurements of Venus actually allowed us to determine not just the size of our own space in the galaxy, but ultimately the size of our own galaxy. Two other scientists in the 1960s, Arniel Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs, were doing what was now called radio astronomy. They were listening to the radio signals coming from outside of Earth. They were working with a small horn antenna system, and they were desperately trying to calibrate it extremely accurately, but they kept picking up a noisy background signal. They looked at every possible explanation for where this background signal was coming from, including the possibility that it was just all the pigeon droppings of the pigeons that were living inside the antenna. So they cleaned it all out and tried every possible way to make the antenna as perfect as they could, but they were still picking up this strange background signal. It just so happens that a few years earlier, the theoretical astrophysicists had been proposing a new model for the formation of the universe, called the Big Bang Theory. One of the things that the Big Bang Theory predicted is that there would be a remnant glow of the after effects of the Big Bang that would be measurable in the microwave part of the spectrum. What this discovery led to was that Penzias and Wilson won a Nobel Prize, because what they were detecting was the cosmic background radiation that had been predicted by the theory of the Big Bang.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Nobel Prize

content: In the 1930s, many people got excited by the prospect of transmitting radio waves into the sky, not just to bounce off of aircraft or storm clouds, but actually to destroy aircraft. These death rays, as they became to be known, generated quite a lot of interest, and even Nikola Tesla claimed that he could build a system that would destroy 10,000 aircraft and blast them out of the sky using beams of radio waves. In the UK, Robert Watson-Watt, who had been working with Appleton on measurements of storm clouds with radio signals, was also approached and asked if he could build a system that could destroy an aircraft and knock it out of the sky. He did some calculations and his result was that you would have to generate far too much energy in your beam in order to destroy an aircraft, but you could certainly detect it. Not only could you detect how far away it was, but you potentially could detect which direction it was coming from. In the 1930s, this was a fairly key moment in Europe, and the prospect of being able to detect aircraft at night time and at great distance was of great interest to the Ministry of Defence at the time. In 1935, Robert Watson-Watt was awarded a patent for a pulsed radar system. At the same time, there were many parts of the world where they were developing similar kinds of radar systems. Not only in the UK, but also in Germany, in America, in Japan, in Italy. Many countries were developing these radar systems, but because they were seen as military systems, they were all being developed in secret. But it's the patent of 1935 from Robert Watson-Watt that is seen as a key turning point in the development of pulsed radar systems.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Patent of Radar

content: In 1941, the American military had been testing radar systems and were still trying to evaluate how useful it would be in a military context. 1941 was also the time, by the way, that the US Navy coined the term radar, radio detection and ranging. But one experiment that happened in Hawaii in 1941 was to convince everybody of the value of radar systems in a military scenario. The team were experimenting with a new radar system up a mountain in Hawaii when they noticed lots of blips on their cathode ray tube. They thought they must have been operating it wrong or there was some kind of noise in the system and were ready to pack up and take it away down the hill again when they noticed a lot of activity and people driving up the hill to announce that the attack on Pearl Harbor had just started. So what they'd seen on those blips was actually the incoming aircraft about to bomb the harbor. That was a key point where it was recognized that the value of radar in a war condition was vital.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Pearl Habor

content: The first really major airborne radar remote sensing project was the RADAM project, the radar mapping of the Amazon. It mapped over 8 million square kilometers of the Amazon. Because the radar system could see through clouds, it meant that there was no area that was obscured. This data has been so significant that even to this day there are still people analyzing some of the data. It's been used for geological mapping, for transportation planning, for timber stock assessment, and was one of the key demonstrators of how airborne radar could be used for many applications of mapping the land surface.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Radam

content: The tremendous success of the first three space shuttle missions carrying radar antennas in their payload bay, Sir A, Sir B, Sir C-EXA, led to the idea to fly an interferometric space shuttle mission. The concept had been tested during the last three days of the October 1994 Sir C-EXA mission. When during three repetitive days, repeat orbits, controlled repeat orbits were flown and the concept that interferometry from space is possible was proven. It took six years until February 2000 when the Shuttle Radar Topography mission took place and within 11 days the whole planet was topographically mapped until 60 degrees north and south, which is the most northern orbit that the space shuttle reaches. SRTM proved that radar remote sensing is capable operationally to map the Earth's topography in a very high geometric resolution.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: SRTM

content: Based on the great success of the C-band radar satellites in the 90s, ERS-1, ERS-2, followed by Envisat-ESA, it was decided by the European Space Agency, jointly with the European Commission, to launch further C-band radar satellites. They are called Sentinels, Guardians. And the first Sentinel-1A was launched in 2014, followed by Sentinel-1B in 2016. These two Sentinels represent a big shift in the paradigm of using space-based radar systems. These data are freely available. They are acquired in an unprecedented high geometric resolution, and thanks to the two satellites in space, we have a global coverage every five to six days.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Sentinel 1

content: In February 2000 the shuttle radar topography mission took place where the concept of spaceborne interferometry was applied, tested and with a marvelous success proved proven. On board the space shuttle were NASA L and C band antennas and an X band antenna developed by the German Aerospace Center jointly with industry. So it was decided by the German government to support in a public-private partnership the development of two X band satellites that would fly in parallel to acquire X band interferometric data sets to map our planet Earth repeatedly until a very high geometric resolution elevation model could be constructed. This was realized through the launch of Terasa X, a German satellite in the year 2007 followed by Tandem X, the second satellite which was needed to perform radar interferometry and was launched in 2010.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: TanDEM X

content: There were two other interesting things that happened at the beginning of the 19th century that influenced scientists' view of light. Jean Foucault showed that the speed of light slowed down as it went through a medium. That kind of put an end to the corpuscular or the particle theory of light and emphasised Young's concept that it must be made from waves. Thomas Young, on the other hand, also demonstrated that waves were transverse rather than longitudinal. So whereas sound waves are pressure waves that move back and forth in the direction of travel and therefore are longitudinal waves, light, that Thomas Young proposed, was transverse so that the oscillation was perpendicular to the direction of travel. This was an important development in the understanding of the properties of light.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Transverse vs. Longitudinal Waves

content: In 1802, a very significant experiment was conducted by Thomas Young. Thomas Young and his contemporary, Augustin Fresnel, were challenging the standard view of light as being made up of small particles. Their view was that light was made up of waves. And the experiment that Young did in 1802 was to take a source of light with a constant colour, so a constant wavelength, pass it through a little slit, so that it directed waves out through that slit, and then put it through two parallel slits. And what he saw in the light on the wall beyond those two slits was a series of bright and dark patterns. And what this meant was that interference was occurring between the two beams of light that went through each of the slits. For Young, this was a demonstration that light was indeed made of waves and not particles. And it changed the perception of how we understand electromagnetic radiation today.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: Young and Fresnel

content: The invention of the telephone had a very significant influence on the development of what ultimately became radar remote sensing. We can have some discussion and controversy over who did or didn't invent the telephone, but it's certainly the case that Alexander Graham Bell got the first patent. In 1876, he patented in America the first telephone system. Alexander Graham Bell, who grew up in Scotland and then moved to Canada and then became American, and then he also helped create the National Geographic Society, and the Bell Company and the Bell Lab still persist and continue with his name. But one of the influences it has on radar remote sensing is that we still have a legacy of using some of the terminology that was relevant to the very first development of communications using things like the telephone. The key thing about the way that you build a telephone is that your sensitivity with your ears to volume compared to the energy of the wave is a logarithmic relationship. As a consequence, the telephone engineers who went on to become radio engineers, who went on to become radar engineers, used a term that was logarithmic, and the unit was the bell, named after Alexander Graham Bell. The decibel is 10 times the bell. To this day, in radar remote sensing, we still persist with using the decibel as one of the units of the intensity of the signal that we measure in a radar system.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: dBs

content: By 1900 the principle of echolocation was quite well known. Ships wanting to detect icebergs for example would make a loud noise with a horn and they would listen for the echoes coming back and the time it took for the echo to come back gave you some indication of how far away the object was. With the development of radio, and Marconi in 1901 had demonstrated that you could transmit radio waves over very long distances, so he was able to transmit it across the Atlantic, is that a number of people came up with the idea of using radio waves as a means of object detection by using echolocation. You transmit a little radio signal and you wait to hear the signal coming back again and the time delay gives you an indication of how far away that object is. In 1904 it was Huelsmeier that developed the first working patentable idea for a ship detection system using radio waves. He'd been inspired after seeing a collision of two ships in the Rhine and a great loss of life and he thought there must be some way to improve the ability to detect ships at night or in fog. His 1904 patent is seen as the first workable solution to doing echolocation with radio.

metadata.video_title: ESA Echoes in Space History: echolocation

content: So, for the supervised algorithm, we have the maximum likelihood. This was probably until recently the most widely used method, and in this algorithm the decision is based on probability. So each target class will be statistically described by what we call multivariate probability density function, and there is an assumption that this function follows a Gaussian distribution. And then each pixel will be compared to the different function. For instance, you have a pixel here, this is a simple example in only one dimension, but so you have this pixel here, and you can see that the probability that it belongs to the class B is higher than the probability that it belongs to the class A, and so it would be assigned to the class B with a certain probability that gives you some confidence index to the classification. And for sure you can work in more than one dimension, you can add several spectral bands in temporal dimension, and then the distributions will become more complex. The main advantage of this algorithm is that there is a full control of you. You can control totally the algorithm, it is easy to understand why a pixel belongs to the class A or to the class B, and if you repeat the same algorithm in the same conditions, you are sure that you will get the same result, which is not the case with most of the training, the auto-supervised classification. The disadvantage is that the assumption that the density function follows a Gaussian distribution is often not true, and so when this is not true, your result can be questioned. And in terms of processing, the disadvantage is that the same set of features shall be used for all the classes, and so you can lose efficiency in your processing because it can become quite expensive. A second kind of supervised algorithm is the artificial neural network. Here, the objective of this algorithm is to mimic the human brain, which is able to see and analyze a lot of information coming from different sources and making link between these datasets, and so the neural network is like what we call a connection of artificial neurons, and this will make the link between all this information. Here, this is a very simple example where you have your input, your output, which are the classes of interest, and there is only one what they call hidden layer, but you can add several levels of layers. The advantage is that this is much more accurate when you have very large datasets than the maximum likelihood. It also supports the fact that the distributions are not normal, do not follow a Gaussian distribution, so this is more robust, and you can incorporate a priori knowledge and some realistic constraints because you can give some input data that corresponds to your area of interest. The main disadvantage is that this is like a black box, and it will be a disadvantage that will come back several times. So here, this is very difficult to understand why a pixel is in one class or in another one. Not the pixel that you know before the classification that this is wheat or that this is barley, but the pixel where you hesitate, the algorithm will tell you this is wheat, okay, you have to trust it because this is very difficult to understand the story. Another kind of algorithm is the super vector machine. So this super vector machine is very popular. I think that with random forest, there are two main ones that are used for the moment with some emerging, new emerging ones. So this is a non-parametric statistical learning technique for solving a quadratic optimization problem. So basically, what it means, so you are working in an input space in a given dimension, and you will, the algorithm will not work with all your training data sets, but only on the training data that are at the edges of the distribution. So the data that will help making the difference between the classes. It will localize these data in your space, dimensional space, and it will try to define the boundary. And this boundary then, based on the training data set, will be used to classify all the pixels of your images. If it is not able to draw a good boundary, let's say, then they will increase the dimensionality of the space by a kernel technique, and then they will work on what they call hyperplan because it can, the number of dimension can increase a lot. At the end, you always have a boundary that will discriminate between the land cover classes. So the advantage is that this is a method which is quite efficient when you have, let's say, small training data sets. So if you do not have, by crop type, many, many samples, this method is robust because it will really look at the edges, and so it does not mind of the full population of training data set. So usually when you, if you have a training data, if you have many, many training data for the read, for instance, you will have a distribution like this. And if you have few training data, if your data set has been collected correctly, you will have a lower density here, but you still should have this representativity in terms of representativity, in terms of variety of practices. So when you have few training samples, you lose the density, but you, we can expect that you still cover the variety of the practices. And so the SVM is efficient in this case, because it is only working with this kind of points in the distribution. The disadvantage is that if you have noisy data, these noisy data are there, typically. And so it will have a dramatic impact on the classification performance, because you will, you think that this is representative, or this will allow to make the difference between the wheat and the maize. And in fact, this is a cloud, for instance. And so this is very, very sensitive to that. Another sensitivity is to the kernel function. I told you that when you are not able to make, to define the boundaries in a certain dimensionality, we increase the dimensionality. The way we increase this dimensionality, if the kernel is not well used, we, there is a high risk of over-fitting or over-smoothing. And so again, the quality, the performance of the algorithm will decrease. We move to another family, which is the decision trees. So here, I think this is rather easy to understand. So this is quite hierarchical. And for each level, you decide, you have a criteria or rule that is tested. And then you decide if you go in one decision, in one tree or in another one. So the advantages are very similar to the artificial neural networks. So under a lot of the measurements, this is robust against the non-normal frequency distribution. It is really easy to apply. You have a few parameters, and the structure is transparent and easy to interpret. So this is not a black box in this case. But the disadvantage is that when you have feature space with high dimensionality, this kind of decision tree, single tree, is very difficult to handle that. And so more and more researches a few years ago have been done in this field of decision tree. And one of the, let's say, result of this research was the random forest. Random forest is also, like the SVM, one of the supervised classification that is mainly used. So this is an improved implementation of this decision tree, meaning that, in fact, it will test different decision tree, and it will combine the results. So how does it work? So for each, they will, in fact, draw different trees with a random subset of your training data. And this is important to have it in mind. So you put your training data, and not all your training data will be used to build your random forest model. So there will be a random sample that will be used. The other ones are not taken. They will do it several times with different random subsets. And then they will decide, finally, for your pixel, the classes that is majority. So there is a majority vote between all the tests that have been done to decide the final level of your class. The advantage is that, for instance, you can cross-validate the results, because not all the data have been used for training. You can use the data that have not been randomly selected to make a cross-validation. So you get quickly an idea of the quality of your algorithm, which is nice. You can also use this information to identify the discrimination power of the different features that you have used. Another advantage is that this is really easy to tune. So there are only two parameters. And the fact that it is more accurate than classical decision tree, because you combine multiple classifications. The disadvantage is also the fact that it is combining a lot of classification made by random subsets. And so this random subset, this is random. Something which is also a disadvantage, and maybe I think for the CAP, this is a big disadvantage. So sometimes there is the need to have something which is repeatable. You should run it several times, and you should get the same output at the end. With this random forest, this is not ensured, because of these random samples that you do several times. And so for most of the pixels where the class discrimination is, let's say, rather straightforward, it will be the same if you repeat. But for the pixels that are the most difficult to map, you may have different results if you run different times.

content: So, let's start with the classification. So, high diversity of classification algorithms split into two main types. So, the unsupervised one and the supervised one. So, unsupervised means that you do not have any a priori information about the spectral signatures of your classes, and so the algorithm will group the pixels together in clusters based on similarities and you will have to label the clusters afterwards. And then you have the supervised algorithm where you use the training dataset to train, calibrate your algorithm a priori, and then you apply this algorithm to all the pixels of your images. For the supervised algorithm, more and more there are some preparatory steps on the training dataset which are cleaned and there can be some iterations between the cleaning of this dataset, you run the algorithm, you look at the accuracy and you improve the training dataset and you go on like this until the output meets your requirements. So, I will present you two unsupervised algorithms. The first one is the K-means. So, the K-means is an algorithm where you need to decide at the beginning how many classes you expect and you arbitrarily locate some seeds at the beginning and then you assign each pixels of the image to the seed which is the most similar. So, you compute the mean in the spectral dimension, temporal dimension, and then you have the clusters. The mean of the clusters becomes the new seeds and then the process is repeated. You reassign all the pixels to the new seeds until you repeat until in fact some convergence is met and so your clusters are rather homogeneous. Another one is the Isodata. So, iterative self-organising data analysis which is very similar than the K-means except the fact that the number of clusters can vary during the algorithm. So, you start with by default numbers but during the process the distance between the clusters are measured. If two clusters are too close then they are merged and the standard deviation of each cluster is also looked at and if the standard deviation is too high the cluster is split. And so at the end this is the algorithm that will decide the number of clusters. But in all cases you need to label the clusters. So, this is really the easy thing. You have different clusters and you need to define which cluster corresponds to each classes but in reality this is often much more complex. You need to work in many dimensions to be able to label correctly the clusters.
