content: There's plenty of ice information that can be obtained from a SAR image, and some that cannot. When an analyst looks at an image of sea ice, they analyze, interpret, outline characteristics of tone, texture, size and shape of the different ice features. The outlined results are then transformed into an ice chart that consists of different regions, and each one of these regions is then coded with an egg code, because it's shaped like an egg. And these egg codes contain information on the amount of ice, in other words the concentration, of the different ice types in each region, as well as the form of the ice, usually the size of the flows. In this example from the High Arctic, we can clearly see the bright, multi-year ice flows that are embedded in the darker tone of the surrounding first-year ice. This information is captured in the ice chart created from the SAR image. This internationally accepted code means that a mariner, anywhere in the world, will be able to understand the ice conditions described by an ice chart. So while a SAR imager is not able to measure ice thickness directly, this information can be derived from the features in the image, and from additional sources. A chart can also include information from other satellite sources, as well as aircraft and ship observations. All these sources of information are utilized by skilled forecasters to create a final product for dissemination. Here is an example of how ice information used by both a shipping operator and by local communities. Let's take a look at the coast of Labrador, where a mining company operates the Voises Bay Nickel Mine. Shipping to this mine occurs year-round, with ice present in the axis from mid-December to late June. Ice first forms in the sheltered bays and inlets of the coast of Labrador, and eventually becomes consolidated. The many islands and rocks off of the coast act as anchors for that ice, which becomes fastened to the land, and is therefore called land-fast ice. This land-fast ice can extend as far as 60 km from the coast in some places, and is heavily used by coastal communities for travel. Beyond the land-fast ice is an area of mobile pack ice that drifts southward from waters further north. Any vessel proceeding to the mine relies on ice information to inform themselves about the ice conditions along the route. The type of pack ice and location of the land-fast ice edge is important to the community, and the mariners as well. The community is interested in the location and state of the ice, the surface roughness, and the location of any areas that have not frozen over because of tidal action. So the people travelling on the ice must be aware of the route and timing of the ship, so that people don't encounter a new broken ship track. In this case, the mining company and the communities work together to mark the ship track and set up a floating bridge over the track that offers a safe and smooth crossing over the broken ice of the track. The various ice information needs of the ship and of the local communities might be different, but in the end they are using the same ice, and it is SAR imagery that is used to chart the ice conditions for both users. Ice conditions are changing rapidly, and SAR provides a historical record and a way to monitor ongoing changes. It used to be that a complete transit of the Northwest Passage was rare due to the difficult ice conditions. But now, since about 2006, cruise ships, pleasure craft, and even commercial vessels regularly make transits of the passage in the summer months. The reason for this is that there is a change in ice conditions, meaning lower concentrations that permit vessels to transit with ease during the summer. This does not mean that every year is easy, but it does mean that there are more easier years. Northerners are concerned by the changes in ice conditions and the impact these are having on their livelihood. Their ability to access traditional spots for hunting and fishing. Their ability to travel to their cabins and to other communities. They're also concerned by ships breaking up the ice when transiting through northern waters. So winter, water, and warming. Yes, ice conditions are changing throughout the year, and we must remember that there is not only less ice in the summer, but less ice in the winter and throughout this cycle. The Canadian Ice Service continues to work with the satellites of the RADARSAT Constellation mission. The promise of compact polarimetry means that the information we gather about the sea ice will continue to improve our understanding of changing ice conditions. I urge you to look at the references and resources listed below.

content: So Ken, is there a way that we could create more generic pre-test tasks? So the idea is basically, for example, if you look up on this slide, you see that you have an image, why don't we combine all these different pre-test tasks and basically augment a single image, the very same image, into different augmentations. But all these different augmentations actually belong to the same image. So basically, we kind of learn that, okay, all these augmentations are actually the same image as compared to a different image. So basically, if you take one image, you create different augmentations, like you distort the image in various manners. And you also, you take another image, which is a completely different image, and then you come somehow, create a way so that you are able to learn the similarity among the same image, which is also distorted. And somehow able to characterize the image, which is completely different from the image which you are taking, which is your original image. So this is actually the idea of contrastive representation learning. The idea is, all these augmented images should have high similarity with your original image, which we could also call reference image, and it should have very low similarity to a completely different image, which is not an augmented one of the same image. So this is like, we could see, for example, this image on below, we could say it is a reference X image, and all the plus signs like X plus, X plus, X plus, X plus are the augmented images. So we should say, okay, the similarity of X and X plus should be much higher than the X similarity of X, X minus, minus means the completely different image. So this is like the whole idea of, as I told you, of contrastive representation learning. So here I would basically showcase one particular, one state-of-the-art, or then state-of-the-art method, which is really well cited in the literature actually, which is based on the simple concept, exactly on the same idea, which is called the CLR, which is simple contrastive learning. And here the idea is that we randomly sample a mini-badge of n inputs X. So to put it simple, let's say, here the X represents a simple image, and we apply two different augmentations to it, and then pass it to our, through a base importer network, and then we have a linear model, which also extracts out, basically uses the output from the encoder, and basically compute the embedding from that. And then both the outputs from both the augmentations, we pass this, basically this main encoder, and the projection head is basically more or less the same for both the augmentations, and we try to maximize the predictions. For example, if I, this XI and XJ are the augmented images of the original X image, and ZI and ZJ are the final predictions coming out of the prediction head, so basically we want to maximize this agreement between ZI and ZJ. So this is like the whole general idea. And how could we do this, basically? So in the paper, they actually used quite different augmentations. So basically, like these are a list of 10 different augmentations which they have actually used to create, so basically they randomly select one of the augmentations to create XI, another randomly selected augmentation to select, to create XJ, and then from there they compute ZI and ZJ, and then try to maximize their agreement. So the way they try to maximize this agreement is basically using this formulation, actually. So they kind of define this similarity between ZI and ZJ using the cosine similarity, which is given by this equation, which is essentially kind of a normalized dot product, basically. And we use this loss function, which is also actually in literature called the info-NCE loss. So noise contrast estimation, actually. And this is like how it, it's essentially a softmax classifier, basically, but here instead of only the logit values, we are using these similarity terms. So essentially, this is a subtle difference in between. And also, and basically this, when we apply this, so this basically gives us the agreement between ZI and ZJs. And we, the final loss here is computed across all positive pairs, that is between all the I and J, and J and I because it may or may not be commutative, the augmentations, the prediction heads, the results coming from the prediction head. So this is like how the general scheme of this CMCLR works. So if we look at the main algorithm, so this is like listed here in a pseudocode manner, so we're basically, we start with the, we sample a mini-batch, XK, and then from XK we draw two augmentations, like T randomly, from T and T dash are the two augmentations, which we apply to our inputs, XK, and from there on we feed it to the base encoder network and then to the prediction head. And afterwards we get ZI and ZJ basically, and from ZI and ZJ we compute the pairwise similarity and compute this info and Z loss. And as a result, finally, once this is done, over a period of time, like after a number of iterations which we want to keep, we only keep the encoder network, which is this F network, and throw away the prediction network. So basically this encoder network F is actually our pre-trained model which we could use to extract out good feature representations for any downstream application. So this is like the learned SSL model. So if I just show you the results which we get for this CMCLR, they are quite surprisingly good actually. So here if you see, this is the graph of basically the number of parameters on the X-axis and the top one accuracy on ImageNet database. And if you see that in the supervised manner setting with 25 million parameters, we are getting roughly around the accuracy of around 77%. And the CMCLR for the same number of parameters is able to achieve roughly around 69%, which is very good actually. But as we increase the number of parameters in CMCLR, the accuracy gradually increases. And basically here, this linear classifier is trained on the representations learned by the feature encoding using entire ImageNet in this particular paper. So with this, I would like to conclude. So I would like to summarize. So what we have seen in this video is we saw what a supervised learning is, how it is compared to self-supervised learning, what is general pipeline of self-supervised learning, and what are three different ways of evaluation methods. For example, we could evaluate using k-nearest neighbors, linear probing, or fine-tuning. And we saw a few examples of pretext tasks. And I gave you an introduction to contrastive representation learning where I went into more detail into this algorithm CMCLR. So thank you very much for listening and have a nice day.

content: So, this is only one example of the pretext task which I showed, but there are many other pretext tasks which people have actually proposed in the literature. For example, in 2016, there was also one very nice seminal paper about these pretext tasks where you kind of create image patches, or maybe nine image patches from an image. For example, here, and then basically you could actually put these image patches in the random order, in the random permutation, and assign that permutation an index. And at the end, basically, you feed these image patches in different permutations to the network, but the network is trained to predict which particular index of the permutation it is, as shown in this figure. So this is a particular pretext task which has been quite useful in literature. The other two, for example, here I show you a pretext task of predict relative position. So here, again, we kind of divide the image into patches, but along with the center patch, we also give the patch to be predicted, and basically here the idea is that where the label is actually, where the patch location is. It's similar to the previous one, but there we are predicting the index of the permutation, but here we are directly referring to the patch itself. And there is also another, on the right side, you could see there is also another pretext task which one could use, for example, image coloring. So here the input image is essentially divided, the color input image is actually divided into grayscale image and A-B color channels. So A-B color channels actually represent green, red, and blue-yellow color components. And then from gray level channel, you try to predict the A-B channels, and similarly from A-B channels, you try to predict the grayscale channels, and then basically from these two, you fuse to have the predicted image, which is the original color image actually. And similarly, two more pretext tasks which I would talk about is basically this feature learning via in-painting, basically where you mask the parts of the image and try to reconstruct them. So here again, you are basically kind of using the same image and reconstructing it. So basically, your feature encoder, which does this job basically, is actually your pre-trained self-supervised model or the feature extractor, which is good enough after training. And similarly, there is also one more, for example, this frame order prediction, where you kind of randomly shuffle the sequential frames and try to predict the order correctly. So this is also one of the pretext task applications. Okay, so if I summarize the pretext tasks, so pretext tasks focus on visual common sense. So it allows the network to learn good features. Performance on pretext tasks is not important, but rather how useful the learned features are for specific downstream applications, for example, classification, detection, and segmentation. They have proven to be really good in vast variety of applications, but there are some small problems. For example, coming in with individual pretext tasks is, of course, tedious, but there are like tons of different pretext tasks out there in the literature. And also the learned representations may not be general.

content: Hi, good morning, everyone. My name is Muhammad Shahzad, and I'm working as a guest professor at the Department of Data Science and Earth Observation at Technical University of Munich. And the title of my talk, which I'm going to give, is basically self-supervised learning, tapping the power of unlabeled data. So this is the outline of my talk. So I will talk about, first I will introduce the supervised learning. And then from there on, I will build foundations of self-supervised learning, that what self-supervised learning is. Then I will introduce you the general framework or general pipeline of how self-supervised learning works. And also discuss some evaluation strategies, how we evaluate self-supervised learning methods. Then I will showcase you some few examples of the pretext tasks, which are actually needed to train machine learning models in a self-supervised manner. Then we will talk about contrastive representation learning. And here I have listed a broad taxonomy of contrastive representation learning methods. I won't go into details of these methods, but one of them, for example, the CLR, I will briefly go into more details of that. So what is supervised learning? So supervised learning is actually learning with labeled data. And this is actually perhaps the type that we refer to when we talk about machine learning. And here the approach is that we collect large data set, manually label the data set, and train the model using that training data. And what do I mean by these labels or the labeled data set is something, for example, on the left, you can see the images, but this could be your input data. And the labels could be, for example, the classification labels. For example, for each image, you know, OK, this image belongs to building, this image belongs to roads, or this image belongs to vegetation. But of course, this is the one particular type of labels belonging to a particular class of machine learning, a particular application of machine learning, which is classification. For example, but there are also many other applications of machine learning. For example, in the detection case, the labels would not only contain the classification label, the name of the object, main object within the area of interest, but also the box coordinates. And similarly, if we talk about segmentation, then the label basically becomes the mask like this. So we have like on the top, you could see on the left side, there is an image of a building from the top view. And then the label is basically a binary mask where we have all the pixels of value one or values in pink, shown in pink or purple that belongs to buildings and the rest all is in black. So this is kind of the label which I'm talking about. And this is actually very good for transfer learning. So where we could take this learned feature representations and like to others, smaller domain specific tasks, for example, classification or object detection, or for example, we could train a model for classification and use those feature vectors in the last layer to train something for segmentation or for object detection as well. So basically, this is referred to as transfer learning. So here, the idea is in self-supervised learning, we kind of want to make these feature representations quite more robust, but without using the label data. So this is all what is all about self-supervised learning. So in self-supervised learning, we do not use the labels directly. So essentially, this is a presentation of learning with unlabeled data. But we somehow learn useful feature representations from this unlabeled data. But the learning still takes place via supervised learning objectives, for example, classification or regression. So this is how I outline how the self-supervised learning looks like. So we have lots of unlabeled data, then we have a machine learning model, and we somehow do some tricks to use unlabeled data and basically build a robust representation of the features. And so somehow, after a few training epochs or something, we are able to generalize some features which are good enough. So how can we do this? So we can do this by solving for pretext tasks in a supervised manner. And labels for these pretext tasks are self-generated in an automatic manner. So I give you an example in the next slide what this pretext task would be. For example, this is an example where I show a pretext task of rotation. So here we could actually take the same image and rotate it to different degrees and then use these rotation angles as our objective. And so basically, we could simply train a model to predict the rotation angle of the rotated images. And if we keep on doing this, then basically we are able to learn good features. So what this means is I show you this by giving you this example in the next slide. So let's say we have this image x, and then we would basically create four degrees of rotation out of this image. For example, zero degrees, this would be one image. Then 90 degrees would rotate this image to 90 degrees. This would be another image. Then we rotate it to 180 degrees. This would become a third image. Then we rotate it to 270 degrees. That would become the fourth image. And here, this y represents the label. So y equals to zero means that this will be all the images with zero degree rotation. Y equals to one means all the images with 90 degree rotation. Y equals to two means all the images with 180. And similarly, y equals three means the 270 degree rotated images. And x always remains the same. So the idea here is that y is kind of a pseudo label, which we have directly generated from the existing data. Here we are not concerned about the exact label of this image. For example, if this is a bird image or what. But rather, from this image, we have created some pseudo labels. And we would use these pseudo labels to actually train our model. For example, now we feed these images to a convolutional neural network, our model, and estimate basically which rotation, if the image is rotated or not. Or if it is, then how degree. So if it is rotated by zero degree, if it is rotated by 90 degrees, this is our objective function. And if we keep on doing this, if we keep on doing this, train our machine learning model, somehow the model, this convolutional neural network model is able to produce very good features, which are useful for many downstream applications, which I will also explain in a minute. So here, we usually don't care about the performance of the self-supervised learning task. This is actually important. For example, we really don't care if the model learns to predict image rotation perfectly. So this is not our task, but by doing so, we are able to, the model is able to learn good features.

content: This is like how, for example, for the repetition, I have made this slide again. So we have lots of label data. We have this model M, a machine learning model, and then we have a pretext task, which we have set. For example, as I showed, for example, image rotation. And we use these pseudo labels generated from this pretext task and train this M again and again iteratively. And after a while, after a few iterations of epochs, this M is able to learn good features. So once we have this, how could we evaluate such features? Let's say we have some features or a presentation which is good enough. How would we evaluate? So one particular approach in evaluation is basically we could assess the quality of features using k-nearest neighbors, actually. So this is one standard way of doing this. So here the idea is that using M, we compute and store the features of the training data for the downstream task, and then nearest neighbor classifier that matches the feature of an image to the k-nearest stored features that works for the label. So essentially, the idea is that you pass on all the training data through your learned model, you get the features, and then basically you store these features. And then you pass on the test data or whatever the data you want to use for downstream application. You use the same model, extract out the features, and basically you simply apply k-nearest neighbors and see, OK, if the model is able to predict correctly or not for your particular application. So this is one way of doing so. But in practice, there are also two other very commonly used methods which have been adopted to evaluate the performance of SSLs. And for example, for this, I will also introduce the downstream task. What this means is we generally define some downstream tasks that are, for example, we want to vertical downstream application could be a segmentation step or an object detection from classification trained model, let's say. So performance of the transfer learning on these high-level vision task estimates the generalizability of the pre-trained SSL model app. So this is like the whole idea. So what this means graphically, this is like this. So basically after the pretext training, we have a pre-trained M, this model, and we kind of do this knowledge transfer. So now we take some small amount of label data and basically use this M to extract out the features and then append a shallow network, a very small shallow network, maybe a linear classifier basically, and then for a particular downstream application. So here, for example, here there are two ways, two general strategies. One is called linear probing. One is called fine-tuning that how could we update the weights when we use this label data for training. One is linear probing refers to fixing the parameters of the learned model M like that which means that we kind of freeze the first encoder part and train a linear classifier on top of the generator representations. This actually helps in measuring how linearly separable the pre-trained embeddings are learned by the model M. And fine-tuning basically refers to training a model on the downstream task by using parameters of the pre-trained model M for initialization. So basically here M is initialized with the pre-trained model weights, but then the weights are also updated for the M itself. In the linear probing case, we fix this M and don't train it, but in the downstream application task, the fine-tuning task or evaluation strategy, we also update the model M weights along with the linear embedding. Okay, so here I just wanted to show how this process like what kind of results do we get when we apply such kind of thing. For example, in this image classifier, I showed you for this image rotation case, setting an image rotation as a pretext task, if we somehow train a model and then we see performance of that model compared to supervised learning models. For example, let's say here the idea is like coming from this paper basically where they applied this used LXNet architecture and did this pre-training on this LXNet architecture and then also compared it with the completely training the LXNet architecture with labels on the ImageNet database. So on the top row, basically this ImageNet labels are the basically it's a supervised in it is done in a supervised setting. So for example, if I concentrate on Conv5 basically, so like the results are shown for Conv1, Conv2, Conv3, Conv4 and Conv5, this means basically all the subsequent layers after that are trained and till this layer the weights are kept frozen. For example, Conv5 means that all the preceding layers weights are kept fixed, but the subsequent three dense layers are updated, like their weights are updated. This is like the standard LXNet architecture. And here we see if we use the ImageNet weights to do the ImageNet labels and completely use them to supervisely train the LXNet model, we get an accuracy of around 50.5. But if we use like and if we do random initialization of the feature extraction and only train the last linear layers, then we are able to get an accuracy of 14.1. So this is like basically the random baseline. And with this RotNet, like for example, using this image rotation as a pretext task, we are able to get, for example, if we see of this Conv5, we are able to get 36.5% accuracy. So you could see much better than the random baseline and approaching to the supervised counterpart. So which is quite promising actually and has actually sparked the self-supervised learning in the community.

content: Out of all the physical units, electromagnetic radiation is one of the least precise parameters which we can measure. When you realize that our measurements come from satellites in space, with a variable atmosphere in between the sensor and the earth, you can imagine that the accuracy of remote sensing data is important to think about. In this clip we will describe the major error sources that influence remote sensing data acquisition and which measures are taken to tackle these errors. A good evaluation of remote sensing products is necessary if you want to draw conclusions based on this data later. Many products are already validated for you, which is handy, but we will also explain some of the best practices in collection of validation data, just in case you still have to do it yourself. Remote sensing data products can be downloaded or purchased at different processing levels. In this table, the product levels for Sentinel-2 are given, and how these data are validated, which we further explain in the next slides. As an end user, you mostly won't start with the raw data, unless you want to do radiometric and atmospheric processing yourself, or work on an application where the radiometry is not essential. For every higher product level, more corrections to the data have been done. Level 1 products are converted to top-of-atmosphere radiance or reflectance. Level 2 products are corrected for atmospheric disturbances. Level 3 products are derived products, so they don't describe the reflectance or radiance at different wavelengths anymore, but for example vegetation indices, LAI products or other variables that can be derived. Vicarious validation is used to validate the radiance measurements of the satellites. This implies that a regular comparison is made between the values recorded by the satellite and measurements done on the ground. For this, large homogeneous areas are used, and surface and atmospheric conditions are measured close to the moment of the satellite overpass. Based on these measurements, the top-of-atmosphere reflectance can be modeled and compared to the satellite measurements. To get an idea of the absolute accuracy, you can look in the mission requirement documents. For Sentinel-2, the European Space Agency aims for a maximum 5% uncertainty. For land applications, we are not interested in top-of-atmosphere quantities, but in the reflectance at the ground surface. This implies that we have to correct for atmospheric distortions through a procedure we call atmospheric correction. The only way to validate the bottom-of-atmosphere reflectance is by doing field measurements. How to collect ground measurements for surface reflectance is explained in further sections. How to validate a level 3 product depends on which kind of data are derived from the remote sensing data. Basically, a good amount of ground-truth measurements is needed. They should have a good spatial distribution and ideally cover the whole range of values that is present in the product. For some products, there are best-practice guidelines for the validation, which can be found in the CEOS protocol. However, such a protocol is not available for all the products yet. A last important point of interest is the size of the area that is sampled. Due to the pixel size of satellite images and the geometric error, we have to make sure that we at least sample an area that can be reliably linked to the correct pixels. Ideally we select large homogeneous areas for this, but those are not always available. When our landscape is very heterogeneous, we have to make sure we sample it in an unbiased manner. For this, different sampling protocols are available, which try to remove the potential bias from the ground data collection. In this knowledge clip, you learned the importance of evaluating sensor accuracy and we gave information on how this is done for remote sensing data, or how you can do it yourself if needed.

content: Welcome back to the second part of the tutorial. I will present you shortly the MLR3 machine learning framework, which we use for modeling the data. You probably have heard of R, it's an open source software, statistical programming language, which is freely available, there's a lot of content in the internet and is often used in spatial data analyses. We will give you some links if you're new to R to get yourself familiar with the language and common methods and common functions to use. In this tutorial we will use remote sensing data to model the grassland surface in this subset I've shown before to see whether the shrub coverage has increased or decreased and in which areas of that subset this expansion happens and to see if there were any controls happening in that area. We do this to this end that if we scale that on a landscape, the users, the farmers can get maps to see if their plots are vulnerable to bush encroachment and to see how much area already is encroached. We are now on the GitHub page of this tutorial. Here we can see a short introduction to what I've already said on the slungbush problem in South Africa. Here we find further resources, for example these pictures or this time series I've already shown. And we find basics on the MLR framework. So MLR, what is it? It's a package, it's basically a universe of packages that uses machine learning algorithms that have already been implemented in R, use them and work with them in an integrated framework, meaning that you don't have to change the interface to an algorithm when you're using MLR because it's sometimes really hard to compare different approaches when using different modeling algorithms. That's why it comes really handy for quick modeling and comparison between algorithms, between datasets and between validation procedures and so on. It is the successor of MLR that has been a machine learning framework before and it's been first released in 2019 and it's still growing, it has a growing community and growing repository. It has different types of machine learning, for example classification tasks, regression tasks or survival analysis. It's fully implemented in the R software as I've already introduced and uses the interface to the learners, so-called learners. For example, the random forest algorithm that is implemented in the Ranger package or the SVM algorithm that is implemented in E1071. In this tutorial, we use random forest. Random forest is a machine learning algorithm that is non-parametric, that means there are no model coefficients involved. That means that we do not do pre-assumptions on our data. That's why it is often used in remote sensing data because it's really, it has, remote sensing data has a lot of dimensions, a lot of unknown correlations. That's why non-parametric models are often superior and random forest is really highly used in earth observation modeling. MLR3 is further useful for tuning models, we come to that in a minute, and feature selection and further methods to compare the models and to make it faster on your device. That's a link to the MLR3 repositorium and now we go quickly into the basics on what a model is. What does modeling mean? A model is an abstraction of the reality. When we do natural sciences, we only have restricted access to training data or data in place. That's why we want to use abstraction of that data and correlations within the data to transfer it to other areas. That's why we model. MLR3 provides a framework for doing that by using different terms. For example, starting with the task or the data, you have data, you can store that as a task, where you specify if you want to do a classification task or regression task and what data input you have. Then, typically, these sets of data are split up in training and test sets. Only the training set is used for training a learner. We've already seen that a learner is an algorithm that uses the data and fits to the data to predict on other data. So the learner is only fitted to the training set, keeping the test set aside. Then the model is built up and predictions can be run. The predictions are usually run on the test set, or if you want to transfer it to other areas, you can use new data to use your model for these predictions. Then you always perform some measures of stability called performance measures to see if the algorithm is working as expected. Repeating all that cycle of modeling is called resampling in this MLR3 wording and is really necessary to see if the modeling has a stable output. In the next step, we will start our actual tutorial.

content: You can find this tutorial on Github. Github is a webpage to share code and collaborate with others. I've uploaded all the code and all necessary information on my Github page, Konstantin Schoenberg in the folder Eocollege Slangbosch. Bush encroachment is a global phenomenon. It has been observed throughout all countries in semi-arid ecosystems, for example South Africa. Bush encroachment means the expansion of woody plants into grasslands, which have before covered only with grasslands. The drivers of that encroachment is still under debate and varies between countries and areas. For example, the rising CO2 level leads to CO2 fertilization that makes woody plants more compatible in contrast to grasslands, so that woody plants start dominating these areas. On the right-hand side, we see a subset of the South African study area. We see the bushes in the western part. This site has been encroached within 10 years of time, which is quite slow in that area. The other parts, we can still see grasslands. Another driver are the extinction of large herbivores. In Africa, this is the regional extinction of, for example, elephants or rhinos, which are known to eat these woody plants. Another driver are changes in the fire regime and land use changes. We can see all these drivers are somehow related to human activities. Some are really local, some are global. In this tutorial, we will analyze the slungbush encroachment in South Africa. Slungbush is a plant only endemic to South Africa, but has been found to invade into native ecosystems, grassland ecosystems. For example, in the area, in the province of Free State. This tutorial is situated between the towns of Ladybrand and Tabaghnu on the border to Lesotho. The area is covered with a mixture of rangeland, which is partly pasture used for livestock breeding and partly are still pristine grasslands and cultivated area for agricultural crops, for example. Now we can see the changing ecosystem in a subset of that area between 2016 and 2021. As we can see, we have rapid changes on different land plots. We can see, for example, black stripes and black areas. These are burned areas and burning is one of the major control measures the people at that site use for tackling bush encroachment and making these areas free again from bushes. Here we can see different images of slungbush from the plant, the top left, that have these long snake-like flowers to large landscapes covered with this bush. On the right hand side, we see control measures the local people use, for example, take them off manually and firing them on piles or burning whole plots of land, really large areas. The goal of this tutorial would be to understand the problem of bush encroachment mapping in savannah ecosystems, on the example of South Africa, and to familiarize with machine learning for earth observation data. Thirdly, to understand the dimensionality of spatial temporal data, and fourth, to conduct a validated spatial classification model.

content:
Welcome, everyone, to the third part of this tutorial on Slumbush encroachment mapping in South Africa. I will first give an overview of the dependencies you need to install or have on your device prior to starting the R tutorial. We need R. The best case is the latest version of it. It's 4.1.2. And we need an IDE, for example, RStudio. We will use RStudio because it's native to R and really good integrated in R. Third, we need QGIS in the end of that session. It's optional, yet it's easy for visualizing the maps afterwards. We need some R packages, starting with Tidyverse, Datatable, Terra, and so on, and these MLR3 packages. Later in the tutorial, I will talk about these different packages and why we need them. R packages are, simply said, a box containing code that make up your toolbox for doing analyses in R. Down here, we have linked to the R primers, if you're new to R, to the, for example, iteration web page I recommend to take prior to doing this tutorial. In the end of this tutorial, we will produce these maps. We can see here a Slumbush probability map from three years, 2015 to 2017, showing the dynamics of bush cover change in that area. Further, we will show how to create indices for showing these results in a single map. I've now opened R, RStudio, and we are now in the first of the three scripts I've provided for you. The first one is called Modeling, and that's where we do a step-by-step guideline how to model with MLR3. At first, I've defined some packages we need for this tutorial, and it's the way to install them is by uncommenting these lines, install packages. I've already installed them, that's why we won't do that now, but for all the others we need to have these packages installed in the R environment. By this function, we will load all the packages defined up here in the current R environment. Down here, we can see them all loading. We can check that everything is correct by typing the all, meaning to check if all the loading worked. Alternatively, you can load the packages manually by the library command. That's the traditional way. We use the tidyverse, that's a convenient library for data handling using so-called verbs. That makes it really easy to wrangle data from different shapes and different formats in whatever we need. The second library is Raster, I've discarded Raster recently because it has been succeeded by Terra. They are subsequent packages, so we are only using Terra today. Terra is much faster than Raster, it has some other priorities. Use sf for vector handling, for example, point data or polygon data. We've already provided for this course. We use mlr3, as I've already mentioned. This is the base package for mlr. We need the mlr3 spatial-temporal package that enables a validation approach suited for spatial data. We need the learners package where random forest is integrated and some others. To compare random forest, we use k-nearest-neighbor classifier, so we have two different results. We can see how the different algorithms work and what predictions they produce. Here we define the base path of this tutorial, which is just where we are now. That's where you've downloaded this package. You do not need to change that unless you transfer the data to another location on your disk, otherwise this is really fine. These are the paths we need later for loading and writing all the data, so we put it now into our environment. This command, the source command, is used to load another script I've provided for you. It's the helper script where these paths are already provided. For the other scripts, we just need to type in the source, helper r, and we are aware of these path variables and other functions I've defined before. This line here is just for creating these paths. You just need to run it once, otherwise it will just output that this path has already been created. In the next section, we will import the satellite data we use for this tutorial. It's Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data. We use the VH Sentinel-1 channel and the SAVI index from the Sentinel-2 data. For both sensors, we use the whole timeline for each year we model. For 2015, only for 2015, and for the following years, only the data for the specific year. Now we search for this data on the disk. In this variable, we've stored now the path to that data set. It's an env stack. We import the layer names of that stack because they are not included into the file itself. By looking into these layer names, we see the beginning of that stack. It starts with SAVI, the Sentinel-2 index, in February 2016 and goes up until September, but there are more variables inside of that stack containing the Sentinel-1 data as well. Now we import the data set itself, stored here in this path, by using the terra command rust. The stack now looks like that. We have this raster class. It has 175 pixels in x and epsilon dimensions and 26 layers, meaning the time steps and the different indices we use. It has a resolution of 30 by 30 meters and this coordinate extent. In this whole story, we use the UTM zone 35 south for the whole analysis that is suited for this South African area. We can plot this data. For example, the first data set looks like this and a Sentinel-1 VH image looks like this. In the next section, I will show you how to import vector files. I've already mapped some areas here. I will show you quickly in QGIS. These are our training data and these are different land cover types I've validated with Google Earth imagery, especially containing that slungbash area here. We use it as the target variable, the variable we want to model for the whole area. Getting back to R, we can use the read sf command from the sf package to load that data. For you, it should be in the same file system as I've introduced before. It's called samples. We can use the command exact extract to index the pixels in the data stack which overlay with the polygons we've previously imported. We get all the data contained in this big raster cube where our training data is. We need that for training our model on that, so we discard all the data that is in the raster stack we don't need or we don't have a label for right now. We will shortly have a look into this training data set. In the output, we can see different classes. We've already seen in QGIS the grassland class, water and forest and also this slungbash area. That's the only one labeled as true for whether slungbash occurred or not. I've chosen a slungbash class for this training data set. I've chosen a slungbash class for this training data set. I've chosen a plot that is covered with slungbash throughout all three years, so for all models we can be sure that we actually see slungbash and not some other grass or whatever area. This is the output when we look on the first row on the extracted data. This is now satellite data. It's a bit messy, but we see the first pixel we have here is not a slungbash area. It's from the grassland and has different values throughout time and throughout sensor and has two coordinates. That's really important here. We included getting the coordinates in this command here. These are again all the variables we have. Now we can look on the dimensionality. It's 638 pixels and 31 variables now in our data set. We filter that only pixels that are covering more than 0.5 percent with a polygon we use, so we can be actually sure that we see the land cover we labeled before. In this line we transfer this data. Now it's still a data frame, a really basic class in R for storing tables to an sf class, so a spatial vector class, where the coordinates are stored in the background and we can use it for, for example, plotting or mlr3 uses the coordinates for registering the data set as spatial data set. This line is only good for transferring the two labels, the class label and the slungbash label, to factorial variables. That's R-specific and sometimes really important if we need a categorical data, a categorical variable that is not a string. Let's quickly look on the data we have using ggplot. In the plots pane now we see the x and epsilon variables and the slungbash areas. This pretty resembles what we see in QGIS.

Now we can decide whether to use the dataset where we provide binary information, so SlangWash yes or no. This is the different colors here, or if you want to do a real land cover classification, so if you want to model for these other classes as well. For this tutorial we reduce it to these two classes, SlangWash and no SlangWash, so we have only the two colors. That's why we discard the class variable now, so that we don't use it for the modeling. Otherwise the algorithm thinks that the class variable is also important for modeling and it will corrupt the whole analysis. That's why we need to discard it here. This line here can be used if you want to perform multi-class analyses with a land cover I've just mentioned before. We now come to the MLR3 sections. First we define a task. A task is containing all the necessary information the algorithm needs for the model. For example the ID, so we give this all a name, we give the backend data we've assigned before, this land cover binary, and we define a target variable, in this case the SlangWash variable. As you can still see here on the right side, we want to model for this SlangWash class. Now we define a learner. A learner is the actual classification algorithm. In this tutorial we test for two different learners. The first one is RandomForest, abbreviated by RF, and the second one is the k-nearest neighbor classifier called knn. Knn is the original package where this method has been implemented, it's from Ranger, and the other one is from kknn. To integrate a learner, you give the name of the learner. In the MLR3 help page we can find all the different classification algorithms, so we can type in the learner we want. We need to put in what we want to predict, it's either probability or only the response. Probability means we also want to know how likely it was that a certain response was found, and response only means we have yes or no decisions. The last variable, importance, is set to permutation. We need that later for assessing the importance of the layers in the model. So we define these two learners, and we found them now as environment variables. For the learners we've declared here, we need to set some hyperparameters. We do this in step 3. For random forest, it is common to take the square root of the number of variables in the model. You can see how many variables there are, it's 71. We take the square root and use just the upper value of that, so we round it up. So this gives 6 for the mtry variable. That means there are the size of split options per tree, it's quite complex, you can look up some videos on YouTube on how to interpret these hyperparameters. The number of trees is set to 300, which is known to be a quite robust estimate. Now we set these hyperparameters in this call, and also for the k and n model. Here a k of 9 was taken. This choice was quite arbitrary, and if you want you can change this k in the way you want. Now in the next section we actually train the model with this call. So we train the random forest model on the data. So this is the task variable we have from above, containing all the data, so all variables. What we want to do, we want to do a two-class binary analysis on the Slangbosch variable, the other coordinates we've given. After we've fitted the learner to our tasks, to our data, we now want to predict on the whole data set, so on the complete geographic extent. I've provided a function for you that takes different arguments, so the task and the model, and where the new data is stored, and the output file. So you can run this function with all the data you need. This contains the prediction of the new data, and the georeferencing of the results, and saving on the disk. It's not much more. So we load the function now. The function is a variable as everything else now, so we can see it here in functions. It's the predict and save function. Right now mlr3 needs to have the new data in a data frame, or a data table. That means we have to coerce all the data, so transform the data from a raster data set to a table, basically. This involves loading it to memory, so if you want to use different data, at this point the computer needs a lot of memory storage. With this example data set, we don't need much. That's why also this step is really quick, quickly done. Now we have all this spatial temporal data set, so the satellite imagery we have loaded as a table. You already know these variables. We can see the different values for each pixel now. In this line, we define the output file for the random forest and the KNN model, and now we just simply call the predict and save function I've defined before. This takes a second. The prediction is now saved to these variables, so we can assess it right now, but also it is saved to disk. That's why we've declared a outfile variable here. In the next section, we visualize our data. So at first, we see what is inside this prediction. On the right-hand side, we see that it's three layers, basically. On the top left, the response, the binary response, so whether Slangbosch or not occurred on that area in this year. The other images show at first the probability that there's no Slangbosch, and in the bottom left, we see the probability that we have Slangbosch. Now we can plot the KNN and the random forest classifier next to each other. Differences between the classifiers are apparent. We see that random forest provides much sharper edges, and the KNN has more scattered results. But still, we cannot quantify which algorithm is better or not. We can just interpret it visually. These plots now show the random forest and KNN classifiers' probability for Slangbosch occurrence. We can see the differences in the two algorithms as well. Now we want to validate this approach. This has been done by splitting the data into training test sets and repeatedly fit the model on this data, on changing training data sets and changing test sets. We do this via repeated spatial cross-validation. This is an approach where the subsets are not chosen randomly, but chosen by subsets in space. Now we can see how this algorithm splits our dataset in different test sets. For example, in the first repetition of our validation, only the red area, this area, is used as test sets, and all the rest is used for training the data. So we can be sure that the data was chosen independently. You can see different lines, which pixels have been actually used, if you want to get more into detail here. We compare this to a simple cross-validation, not spatial cross-validation, where the pixels are just chosen by random. This looks like that. You can see the cross-validation that is non-spatial. That means the training and test sets have been chosen just by a random choice. We do the same for the KNN model. And now in this section, we actually perform the resampling, it's called, the validation. This resamples training and test sets as many times as we've defined beforehand. We've defined 10 folds, 10 repeats, means we repeat all the approach 10 times on 10 different subsets of training and test. So 10 times 10, 100 times for each algorithm. This now takes a while and maybe your computer is getting to the limits. If this process takes too long for you, you can always reduce the number of repeats and folds I've defined up here to adjust it to your computer. Using the measure, as in the MLR3 quick start we've shown before, we use the accuracy. Using the simple non-spatial cross-validation, we reach an accuracy of 99.4%, yet this is a biased estimate because for spatial phenomena, it is not liable to use pixels right next to the one you want to predict or want to validate because of the spatial, so-called spatial autocorrelation. If you want to know more about spatial autocorrelation, you can refer to Brenning et al. 2012. So you know why we use spatial cross-validation here to have an unbiased estimate. The spatial cross-validation has an output of 93.2%. It is far worse than the non-spatial cross-validation, but it is more suited for the data we have. We can go into the first lines of the scores, so the first 10 repetitions. We can assess how these performed. We can see that lots of them performed really well. So the error, this is the error, not the accuracy, but they are basically the same, but just 1 minus the error is the accuracy. We see that a lot of models have 100% accuracy or zero error, but some have some error. This is a problem of the dataset we have. If you have more scattered data, you are likely not achieve 100% accuracy in some repeats, but have a more stable estimate. It's part of this dataset that we have a little bit.

high variance in the result. The KNN has also a really good estimate, but this KNN for example is really bad in transferring the data to a new dataset. That's why we can see it on the maps that KNN has these more scattered outputs and shows some errors. After we've assessed the accuracy of our model it is sometimes really interesting to know why a certain model fits like that or which variables have been important for the model. That's why in this step we use the MLR3 filtering algorithms to see what features so which dates and which layers, which satellite data was actually important for the model. Here we fit a filtering variable. Now we calculate the performance of the different variables and store it back into this filter variable. To look into these results we transfer it to a data table and we can plot it using the MLR3 autoplot functions. On the right hand side we see now which layers have been important for the model when we use all the data we have and not splitting into test and training set, but using all data. We see that the Sentinel-1 VH is the most important layer in the model, so explaining the highest deviance of the phenomenon Slangbush, non-Slangbush. It is in the February so in the southern hemisphere summer, as well as the second layer. It's a Sentinel-2 based index in March. Sometimes we want to visualize that differently. We can extract the dates from these layers and layer identity which can show it on a timeline. The most important layer was this VH in March and this Sentinel-2 based index. Now we see different importances here, but note that if the layers are close to each other, the importance may be leveraged because the same data is shown in the next one right after or in the one before. Also maybe that's why the March acquisition has the highest importance because there's no data around that. But this is still interpretation. This has been the first part of the practical session. In the next one we will look into how to automatize this whole procedure to do training and prediction for the other two years and produce change maps.

metadata.video_title: Slangbos Mapping - Slangbos Mapping Tutorial 1/3

content: Welcome back to the second part of this tutorial. In the first part, we've seen how to import spatial data into R, especially raster data and vector data with the packages Terra and sf. Secondly, we've seen how to extract a training and test set from spatial data, satellite data. We've seen how to set up a model with MLR3, how to set hyperparameters, how to train and predict new data from that model, for example, an entire satellite scene. And we've seen how to assess models by performing cross-validation. And at last, we've seen how to assess the importance of single features in the model. Now, the second script is for automatizing the tasks from the first one. So we use the functions we've already defined, but boil it together to functions we can iterate for each year we want to predict for, so for the years 2016 and 17. At first, we load the packages as shown also in the first script. We load the helper file containing all the paths. Then we import the data, or we query the data on the disk. We can look into that file and we see all three dates, 2015, 16, and 17, in nvstack files. We import the layer names as well, and then we import the data in a vectorized manner. That means that we iterate over all paths we have found on the disk and load it separately and store it into a variable called rasters containing three raster files in all three slots of the list. And we can see those three rasters inside. Now we import the training data again. That's the same step as we've seen before, containing the different land cover types and slung wash areas. So in this function, we extract all the training and test sets for all three years. So this returns a list of length three again. So for each year, 2015 to 17, one list entry of extracted satellite data. Now we select only the slung wash class that is false true. That's what we've done in the script before as well, to only classify based on the existence of slung wash or not. If you want to perform a multi-class analysis, I've supplied also the function to only select the land cover variable. In this section, we find a large function. Don't be scared of the size, but it makes it far more convenient to iterate, to loop through all the years we have, so all the data instances we want to model for. So at first, we uncomment this block here. That is not necessary, but for showing you how the variables inside the function work, we subset all the... we input... we select input data for the function before. So we take the first year, 2019, the first training set. We have the learner ID, the random forest algorithm, and the target variable slung wash. We have the coordinate reference system, and the outfile for the data, and a list of hyperparameters we want to input. These are all variables we can input in a function, and as we see later, we can iterate over these. But now, using these variables, we can go into that script. So at first, we start a task. We call it automate in this case, but the ID is basically arbitrary in that case. We have the backend data, that's a training set, and the target variable, and we can look in how the task looks like here. We have again the target variable slung wash, all the variables in the model, and the coordinates. In the next step, we define a learner. That's the random forest learner. We can print it, we can assess what is inside this learner, and what the learner is capable of. We set the hyperparameters. These can be tuned in another step, but it's not part of the course. You can look on the resources on MLR3, on the MLR3 book. There's a lot of information on hyperparameter tuning that is more important when using other machine learning algorithms than random forest, for example. Then we train the learner. We use the new data to predict, and what is now the output of this g-referencing function is a raster that contains the response variable and the probability maps. Basically, now it's just written out on the file, on the disk. Now we can comment this block again. We don't need it anymore, because we will iterate over these settings here. We load in this function. In this block, we only make new filenames, so that new files can be written to the disk that have a different name than the incoming files. Using that function, model and save, we now run that chain we've defined above. We can see all the command line outputs here. It's really easy to assess if everything went fine or not. You can see the sample size and the hyperparameters we've set, and also a random forest-specific error measure, where we can assess if the model is good or not. Now we iterate over all the years with this function pmap. Pmap is like map, but takes a list of arguments and iterates over each of them. We iterate over the rasters, so the new incoming whole satellite scene. We iterate over the training sets of each year and iterate over the out files. This can take now a second to run. There was an error, but I think it should run. Now all three years are predicted and already saved to disk. When this is finished, we can quickly visualize that with the plot function, the native rplot function. Now on the right hand side, we see the response layer random forest produced for each year. This is starting with 2015, 2016, and 2017. We already see some dynamics in that, but in the next script, we will see how to visualize that more appropriately and also go into QGIS to make some fancy maps. you

metadata.video_title: Slangbos Mapping - Slangbos Mapping Tutorial 2/3

content: Welcome to the last part of the tutorial. In the second one before, we've produced the predictions of slungbush occurrence on our study site for three different years. In this part, we will visualize this data using QGIS and R. First we start in QGIS. That's actually what I recommend to look on the data before using them. That's a data stack which is really huge, containing all the data from the first date to containing VH and Central 1 and Central 2 data likewise. In red, we see the training sets we've defined. And now we import the model results into QGIS, going back to R. We import two packages. This is now really slim, because we only want to visualize using ggplot inside the tidyverse and using Terra for raster imports. This line is for setting up a ggplot theme that is really clean, but you can choose any you want or keep it as default. Here we again query for the prediction for the data on the disk that we import in this statement. So now again, we have a list of three spot raster files containing the predictions we've exported in the last script. Now we extract only the third layer in that. We can see it has three layers, the probability of false, the probability of true, and the response. The first two are float variables, meaning that it has data from 0 to 1, but all the steps in between and the response only is true and false. At first, we are only interested in the actual response in the binary prediction. We give these the three raster names of the years and we plot them. This exactly resembles the plotting from the last script containing the response variables. In this line, we save these response variables to the disk. We can now change to QGIS and load this data. I have it already in this environment, but you can use the Slangbash basemap that's also provided on GitHub for convenience. There are already all the layers inside. Otherwise, you can just go inside your college Slangbash folder, go into data, results, and that's everything we will learn in this script. We are using now the response geotiff. We at first see nothing, but if we change the visualization to just simple grayscale, we have three layers, 2015, 16, and 15, 16, 17, containing exactly what we've seen in R. Now we get back to R. It makes it sometimes troublesome if we have temporal changes, temporal data to visualize in just one map. That's why when we have three time steps, it's really easy to create something like indices for each time so that we can visualize it by using categories for each year. At first, the first year we keep as it is. It contains a one for a true Slangbash response and a zero for a negative. We multiply the second layer with 10 so that a positive Slangbash occurrence is 10 and a negative zero, and the last one times 100. That creates certain indices for each year. Now we add them up so we have data from 0 to 111. All the combination of years has its own index. Now we switch back to QGIS to visualize these indices. What we see now is a background map of the data stack we have. In the far background, there's a QGIS base map. On the right-hand side, we see what these indices mean. So zero means that in each year, no Slangbash occurred. I've marked that as transparent so we can see through on our data stack. So a large share of this area that was never predicted a Slangbash occurrence. It doesn't mean that there was no, but our algorithm plus the satellite data we used cannot detect or is only feasible of detecting as Slangbash as we see here with the given data and the training sets. Now the red one means that Slangbash only occurred in 2015. These large areas mean after 2015, these areas disappeared. So they've been probably burned. We know from this area that there has been a lot of Slangbash control happening. So it's pretty likely that there has been human intervention to get rid of this Slangbash coverage. Now the orange tones mean 2016 and 2015 to 16. These are transition classes where there was Slangbash coverage in two years. The green one is only 17, so the last one. This is visible in the northwest part here and down here, meaning that there has been bushes growing, which is quite interesting that it's so dynamic, so fast encroaching into these areas that it's only been detected in the last year. And the dark blue areas have been covered by Slangbash all the time. Here on the right hand side in blue, we see the training test area. We've trained our algorithm on. That's why we have an extreme overfit to Slangbash occurrence. That's why it has been here for 100%. But we have used this area for a reason. As we see on the base map, there is a huge coverage still in the last year. But now in most recent, there has been Slangbash control happening. That's why for new data, we would need new training sets or algorithm. But for the time we chose, 2015 to 17, this is enough to take an area that has been continuously covered with the land cover type we want to detect. Now we get back to R again and map the probabilities. These are encrypted in the second layer. We remember that it contains the probabilities, false and true. We only use true and false is just the same, but one minus the true probability. So it's enough to just take one, extract it from each year and give it a name as well. On the right hand side, we see simple R plots of the probability through all the three years. Now we want to visualize that with ggplot. ggplot is a library included in the tidyverse. That's the meta package we've loaded in the beginning of the script. That contains a large library of visualizing data and also maps. That's why we use it here. First, we have to transform our data to a data frame. Also the raster data has to be transformed to a data frame to be processable for ggplot. That's what we do here. Then we transform it into the longer format. You can look it up on the R web pages and help pages what this means. Now we can use ggplot on that data using geom raster. Typing in the x and epsilon coordinates and using fill as the variable for the probability values. On the right hand side, we see panels of all three years. Now a little bit screwed because of the size of the R editor. But if we squeeze it like this, they are actual rectangle maps. Now we want to export the three maps to the disk so we can use any photo or visualization software around using png. First we split all the data per year so we only plot each year. Now using again map to iterate all the three years. And we print the three maps we've already seen. Now with this arrow you can go back and see all three maps. Using ggsave, we can take these maps and write them onto the disk. The maps we have exported here were used on the web page to create a short animation of the three years. You can do this in R as well, but a simple give maker in the web also does the job. Looking into that map, we see huge differences per year and changing areas where slugmash has occurred or disappeared. That's pretty similar to what we've already seen in the indices, but now it's a bit more dynamic. We see that this area is really sprawling in 16 and 17 and the middle area is being cut down or controlled much more. We can have an idea of the fast expansion of this invasive species into these formerly agriculturally used areas or used for rangelands and livestock breeding.

metadata.video_title: Slangbos Mapping - Slangbos Mapping Tutorial 3/3

content: Let's now have a quick look back to the beginning of the tutorial. The objectives were to understand the problem of bush encroachment in savannah ecosystems. I hope we could show that the high dynamics in these ecosystems pose threats for the farmers and are a major biological change in these ecosystems. Secondly, I hope we could familiarize you with machine learning in general and machine learning for earth observation data, for satellite data, and introduce you to the MLR3 package that is still evolving and will in future make it easy for you to model large scales of data, for example for mapping invasive species or mapping land cover types or whatever tasks you need. I hope you understood that the dimensionality of the data, that it's both spatial and temporal data and the way we split it, we split it into training sets and we split it into yearly slices, that's all also arbitrary. You can decide for yourself, for your data, what subsets you need, what training sets you need and where you have the data availability or if you want to take the whole temporal timeline of data or you have biannual or somehow else temporal data. At last, we've conducted a validated spatial model. That's important because the simple non-spatial cross-validation gave us an optimistic model assessment but by validating it spatially we have a more realistic view on how good the model performs on the task land cover classification task we did. I hope you enjoyed the tutorial and we'll see you again on EO College. My name is Konstantin Schoenberg and goodbye.

metadata.video_title: Slangbos Mapping - Summary

content: Hello and welcome everyone to this tutorial on bush encroachment mapping in South Africa. This tutorial is part of the Dry Ecosystems course of EO College. I am Konstantin Schellenberg from the Friedrichsschule University of Jena. I'm a postgraduate student at the Chair of Remote Sensing and I will guide you through this tutorial.

metadata.video_title: Slangbos Mapping - Welcome

content: Today we are standing in our forest test site. This test site is located about 30 kilometers southeast of Jena and we are here at a 320 meters above sea level. This forest, like most forests in Germany, is a managed forest. So we are here in a pure spruce stand, Picaea abies, the Latin word. The trees are about 50 to 55 years old and reach a height of 20 to 25 meters. The geologic subsurface is made of red sandstones and most soils here are pot soils or brown pot soils. The average yearly temperature reaches 9.5 degrees Celsius and we have an average precipitation period of 700 to 750 millimeters. This network consists of 27 measurement locations and at each measurement location we have eight sensors installed into the soil. At each measurement location we have eight sensors into depth and they are installed in the four directions, north, east, south and west. The measurement stations measure every 15 minutes and the data are stored in SD cards internally. The data stored in the measurement devices can be read out by a mobile computer. And how this is done we will show you in the next minutes.
