content: Now that we know how the TDR measurements are working in theory, we want to do a little experiment. So we have a handheld TDR device, we have a plant and we have water and I will measure the soil moisture content using this TDR device now and then we add some water and then we measure again and if we are lucky the TDR measurement device will show us an increase in soil moisture. So we added some water to this flower pot and now I will take a second measurement of soil moisture using this TDR device. So I insert this sensor unit with the waveguides into the soil and I press the read button at the device and now we have 41.2% of volumetric soil moisture after adding water to the soil.

metadata.video_title: Soil Moisture Estimation - Lab: Measuring soil moisture

content:
Okay, so hello everybody. My name is Marcel Urban. I'm from the Department for Earth Observation at the Friedrichsschule Universität Jena. And today's practical is about calculating a surface moisture index from Sentinel-1 time series and comparing it to actual in-situ soil moisture measurements using R. As already mentioned in today's tutorial, we are utilizing Sentinel-1 time series, so radar data with C-band, so the wavelength is approximately 5 centimeters. And we are using the VV polarization as the VV polarization is sensitive to surface moisture changes. So we're using a time series. And in this specific case, we have an acquisition of a Sentinel-1 scene every 12 days. So when we look right now into our R program, we see that at first we need to install and load some packages we need to import to the program for our calculations. And these packages are mainly used for raster handling and also plotting of data. So at the beginning of our R script, we need to install or if they're already installed, load some packages, which were then used for the handling of our raster data. So basically importing and reading the raster data as well as for plotting our data then in the end. And here we are using a package called Pacman. And Pacman is very useful if you have a lot of libraries you want to load at the beginning of your script, which is in this case here, this list of packages we want to load. And so we import the library Pacman first, and then with the comment pload, we're importing all of the libraries. So in the next step, the next part of the script is basically doing the import of the raster data. So as I said, we are using Sentinel-1 time series and VV-polarization with a temporal resolution of 12 days. And in the first step, we are setting a folder where the data is stored with a comment set vd, wd. And then we know the name of the file, which is this one here. And the data is actually based from a small nature reserve in Southern Africa. And we are importing the file with this comment, with the comment brick. And actually, this is an envy file. So an envy file is containing the raster information, but also the band name information. This is very important for the next steps because we want to import information from the individual band names because they are named after the date of acquisition. So as it is satellite data, we also need to handle no data values because there are some gaps in the data. In this specific case, we don't have clouds because it's raster data. So the cloud, the raster radar signal penetrates the clouds. But we also have other artifacts. We might also have other artifacts in the data. And we know that this value of the artifacts of the no data values are minus 99. So we define that for the R script as NA, which is then known from R to be the no data value. The Sentinel-1 data are actually in logarithmic decibel values. And with the logarithmic scale, it's difficult to make some calculations to apply some equations on the data. So we want to transfer that at the beginning of the script here to linear values in order to make the right calculation with the data. As it is now imported and it is a, here you see it as a file, a raster brick file, for example, and contains some different metadata information like the amount of layer and the extent of the layer. We want now to save this data set here, the raster brick, as a data frame because it's more easy to handle in R to have an own data format of the data. And we do it by this comment. So right now we have a new variable which is called DF data frame. And as I said before, we are using an NP file here. So what we want to extract right now is the band names from the data frame. Because I said in the band names, we have the information of the date of acquisition of the satellite image included. So we're doing it here and then I can open this new variable band names. And we see a list actually. And this would be the last entry in the list. This is the band name from the NP file. And it contains actually here the information on the acquisition date. So this would be the 4th of September 2021. And behind that, behind the date stamp, we have some information on the polarization here and some information on the processing steps which have been done prior to this analysis. So what we want to do next is we want to extract this part here of the names because we want to get only the date of acquisition. And we're doing with this for loop here. So that means we have a new variable right now which is called date. And if I open that, you see that the list has shortened and each entry in the list has changed and we only have the date information. But these are only numbers right now. But we know that is the date. But what we want to do is we want to transfer this number right now to a date format which is recognizable by R. So in this we're doing with this comment posixct where we define how this data frame, where we define how this date looks like. So we have this information here that it starts with the year, then the month and then the date. So if we define it and starting this in the for loop, we're getting actually a new variable right now which called date sent in a one, date as one. And if I open that, we see that the date format has changed. And this is right now a date which is recognizable for the R script. This is very important when it comes to plotting afterwards. So after importing the data, we want to actually retrieve the surface moisture information from the sent in a one time series. And we are doing this with the change detection approach and the reference to this approach you can find in the additional information. So first of all, we need to calculate percentiles. So we are using not the minimum and the maximum. We are using the percentile five of the data and the percentile 95. And we are defining first function to calculate these percentiles. And with this functions, we can define the data which will be imported to calculate the percentile. We say that no data information we defined a prior will be not taken into account. And we can define which percentile we want to calculate. So this would be the percentile five and this would be percentile 95. In the next step, we're using this function for the calculation actually to define two new variables, the perc five and the perc 95, which is basically then executed with a command calc, the file we imported and the function we defined. We are using the percentiles five and nine because we are searching for a wet and a dry reference. And this is important for the change detection approach. So because we assume that radar backscatter which is low comes from a surface which is dry and the backscatter with high intensity comes from a surface which is wet. So that means we are having a dry and a wet reference because we are searching for the lowest backscatter and the highest backscatter in our time series. And with this, we can compute the range between these wet and dry conditions. And afterwards, we are using this equation for each pixel where we take the actual value of the time step minus the dry reference divided by the range of the wet and the dry reference multiplied by 100 to retrieve actually percentage surface moisture information. So actually, we're getting a data set right now which is scaled between zero and 100%. And as there might be outlier in the data which goes above 100% or below zero in the data due to artifacts in the data, which might be very rare, we then eliminating this information, so values above 100 and values below zero in the data file here in the new variable soil moisture. So and this would complete the next step calculation of the surface moisture and the executed code with one click. So as I said in the beginning, we want to compare our surface moisture derived from our satellite data to real in situ measurements from soil moisture network which was installed in March 2020 at the Ben Fontaine Nature Reserve. The soil moisture probes there measure the soil moisture every half an hour in a depth of six centimeters. And this is the data set we want to compare to our satellite information. So what we first need to do is we create a new variable which called data and we read a text file because the data which comes from the in situ soil moisture probes is a TXT file and we import this data with this command. And as we know how this table is structured, we will give each column a name. And the column names are basically it starts with the date, then we have an ID of the first probe, the first sensor, we have different measurements, the temperature, the soil moisture, and the battery voltage for each of the sensor and we have eight sensors in total at each side. As we know how the table is structured, we define the names of each of the columns for the future analysis of it. So we know that the first column is actually the date. The second column is the ID of the sensor and our soil moisture network there consists of eight sensors and they are all connected in one data logger. And these eight sensors are in each direction on 10 meter cables. So that means we have a 20 meter diameter of our soil moisture equipment there measuring the soil moisture at each of this direction. Okay, in the next step, we want to prepare the table we imported for the future analysis. So because we don't need information on actually the ID of the sensor or the battery voltage which is included in the table, we actually create a new table which only has the important information in it. So the first thing what we do is we extract the date from the first column into a new variable which actually called data date. And it looks like this. You see actually the date and the time. As I said, the soil moisture information is measured every half an hour. In the next step, we select the soil moisture from the data file. And here we can select that with

this string, which called SM. So each column, which starts with SM, Soil Moisture, will be selected and put into a new variable. And these are right now eight sensors. So the new variable consists of these eight columns right now. And then the next step, we want to combine the Soil Moisture information and the date to have a new table. And this is done with the command cbind. We see that we have a new variable right now, which is called dataSoilMoisture. And we see that we have now a table, which has the date at the beginning and then all the eight probes after the date. And we also want to do it for the temperature. So we make the same approach. So we select all the columns, which start with temp, creating a new variable. But we don't want to have the temperature of all the eight sensors. We want to create a mean out of it. So we actually calculating with the command row means the mean temperature of this moisture network there. And we can then see that it's only one value left. So that would basically the temperature at the sensor. So that means in six centimeter depth, the temperature of the soil for each half an hour. So and similar to the conversion of the date, which we have done for the Sentinel-1 time series at the first part, with the posixct command, we do it also for the date included in our new tables. And this would be done with this command. So we're creating first a new variable, which is called D underscore T, converting the dates to our known format, and then overwriting the date column at each of the new variables for the soil moisture and for the temperature. So right now, we have created a data frame for our satellite information and converted it to surface moisture information. And we created a table, which consists of in-situ, so ground soil moisture measurements and temperature. So and what we want to do right now, we want to plot them. First, we have a look at the soil moisture information, which have been measured by the in-situ soil moisture network. So there we want to prepare the plot right now. And we define the limits of our plot. So basically, the start and the end of our x-axis, where the date is shown. So when we're doing this with a new variable, which is called limbs. So then it comes to plotting the data in the next section. And first of all, we define the name of the file we want to export. So we want to export the plot as an image. So we can do it as a png in this case here, or as jpeg, or as tiff. So we define it as this file name here, soil moist temp Ben Fontaine png. It will be saved to the folder where our data is. We set initially. The next step would be, we define a start time of the plot, which is actually the first entry of our variable limits. So it will be the 1st of March 2020. And we of course define an end time, which is the second entry, which would be the 1st of December 2021. There's a parameter, which can be set how the dimension of the plot should be. And then we have the plotting command itself. And here in the plot command, we define what should be on the x-axis, which is the column date, and what should be on the y-axis, which is the column temperature. We can define also a main title of the plot and several other information. For example, what is the caption for the x-axis, and what is the limits for the y-axis. So there are several things we can do. So now we plot the data. And we see at first, we plot only the temperature. And as I said, there are eight sensors measuring soil moisture information. We add each of the sensor by a separate line. And they are listed here separately. So it's more easy for you in the end to handle changing of color, changing of line type, changing of line width. And you see right now, so we added all the eight sensor informations here. And right now, we're creating a background grid to make it better readable between these axis entries. So and we also want to add a secondary axis right now, because we have soil temperature and soil moisture. So on the second axis to the right would be the soil temperature in degrees Celsius. And on the left axis, on the first axis, would be the soil moisture in volumetric percent. And that we know what line is what, we add a legend to the plot, where we see now that the black dashed line is the soil temperature. And the colored line are each of them showing in the information of a different probe of a different sensor. So now an x-axis is missing where we see the dates. And so as we defined which is the start date and the end date, we can label them here very easily with text. And we see that actually, if I make it a little bit bigger, it's updating so that we see that here starts with the March of 2020 and end on the December 2021. Okay, so within the next step, we want to plot our in-situ information here, in-situ soil moisture information, to our satellite-derived surface moisture to compare what is the fit between the satellite signal and the actual measurements from the ground. So what we need to do first is we need to combine these two sources, which are pretty different, because the satellite made an observation every 12 days, and the in-situ measurements are taking place every half an hour. So what we in the first site need to do is to actually calculate a daily mean of the in-situ soil moisture information. And in the same step, we're also combining all the eight probes to one value. And what we all need to do is to apply, to make it more comparable, to apply the change detection approach to the in-situ soil moisture information. And this will be done with this formula here. And we create each time a new data frame, which will be then utilized for the plotting of the data. So that means we're making calculations which will be then utilized for the plotting of the data. So that means we're making calculations, we're copying this to a new data frame, and we're adding the date, because the date is very important for the plotting in the end, because we always need to know at which date this value is coming from, and if it's a Sentinel-1 derived surface moisture index, or if it's an in-situ measurement. In the next step, we actually transpose our satellite data, because the satellite data, when we imported it as a data frame, it is not a table where each column shows the time series of the pixel. In this case, each row is showing the time series of the pixel. So that means in here, we have a raster data set, which has a dimension of three by three pixel. So that means we would have nine rows, and columns would be actually the dates. So what we need to do, we need to bring it also to the same dimension we have in the same order we have for the in-situ measurements. So that means we need to transpose this table of the satellite-derived surface moisture by this command here, T, which means transpose, so that we have our pixel information in each column and the dates in the row. As I said that we have three by three pixel in the raster file, we want to calculate the mean of these nine pixels. And we're doing this with this function here, which is actually calculating the median from these nine pixels. And we also want to have the standard deviation, which will be used for the uncertainty in the plot. So yeah, we're calculating the median of the nine pixels, and we're calculating the standard deviation of the nine pixels. And the median will be shown as a point or rectangle then in the plot, and the standard deviation as arrow bar. And in the end, we're saving everything in a data frame. As we are using the ggplot function for plotting our data, and ggplot is very useful and is widely used for plotting when working with R scripts, we first need to melt the tables, which actually put all the columns on top of each other. So in the next step, we actually execute a ggplot command, which will then plot the in-situ soil moisture information on top of the surface moisture information derived from the sentinel one-time series. So, and ggplot is developed consecutively, so you can change different parameters in the plot in each of these lines. So basically the title, the axis title, the axis length, the plot size, and if you want to integrate a line or a point or this arrow margin, and this is all included here in the next comments. And actually it is plotted in the end, so we execute all of these comments here. And in the end, we execute the P, and we see actually here that this plot shows the in-situ soil moisture in percent, in blue, and the sentinel-derived surface moisture information, so the surface moisture index every 12 days. And we see actually it's a very nice fit, even or especially for the dry-out phases here after precipitation events, so the precipitation events can be seen as peaks here in the data, and the satellite signal actually pretty much react on that, and also in the dry-out phase we have a very nice transition of the information. And in the last comment, we can plot, we can save this plot to a file in our folder. Okay, so this is the end of the tutorial. So what we learned today is to convert Sentinel-1 VV-polarized time series into surface moisture information, and compare it to in-situ information, actually ground measurement, and plotting them, and saving these plots to a specific file. Thank you.

content: Now we are at one of our 27 in-scene tourism measurement sites and we want to show you how data are read out. There is one sensor in each cardinal direction at two depth levels. Every one is located at the top of the first mineral soil horizon. The second layer is located approximately 10 cm below. In total there are 8 sensors at each measurement site. The 8 sensors are connected with a so-called end unit. This device controls the measurement process. It contains a battery, a microprocessor and an SD card. Every 15 minutes a measurement is started and the measurement data are stored at the SD card. The end node is installed inside a plastic tube which is painted in green for camouflage. With a special tool the lid of the tube is removed and after that the device is taken out. Now the end device is opened. This is done by removing six screws which hold the upper and the lower part of the end device together. Now the download of the data from the device can begin. Before it is connected to a field notebook the device is switched off. Then a special cable is used to connect the measurement device to the field notebook. And a computer, a software to set up and read out data from the devices installed. Once the data are downloaded from the device they can be used for further analysis in the office. For instance they can be compared with Sentinel-1 radar data to test if there is a relation between soil moisture and radar backscatter or for other research questions like forest ecology and local hydrology.

metadata.video_title: Soil Moisture Estimation: In the field - How to read out soil moisture information

content: The network has been installed to get soil moisture measurements under forest over a long period of time. Why we are measuring soil moisture? Mainly we are not interested in the soil moisture itself. We are mostly looking at radar images and at radar backscatter time series. We want to measure all kinds of environmental variables to interpret the radar backscatter and we want to see if there are phenological cycles or any other temporal patterns in the data.

metadata.video_title: Soil Moisture Estimation: In the field - Why we measure soil moisture

content: Hello, my name is Carsten Pater, I'm working here for the Department of Earth Observation. I studied geography and after my studies I went to Vienna in Austria, did my PhD at the Technical University with Professor Wolfgang Wagner on somatosensory retrieval from envisar data and then I returned to Vienna and working here for the remote sensing group, I'm mainly working with radar data and the retrieval of biophysical parameters like soil moisture or biomass. Today I want to speak about soil moisture retrieval, how it can be measured and what is the physical background of the measurement, especially the TDR measurements. First of all, let's have a look at the soil. What is a soil? A soil is a weathered and fragmented outer layer of the Earth's terrestrial surface and it has been formed initially through the disintegration, decomposition and recomposition of mineral material contained in exposed rocks by physical, chemical and biological processes. They are further conditioned by the activity of organisms, plants and animals and in the end it culminates in deformation of a characteristic soil profile. Every soil contains water and soils are in fact a mixture of solid, liquid and gaseous constituents like minerals, organic matter, water and air and under natural conditions nearly every soil contains some amount of water. Soil moisture is the volume fraction of water held in the soil against gravity or another definition is soil moisture is the amount of water which evaporates within 24 hours when drying soil samples at 105°C. So why is soil moisture that important? Well, the knowledge of soil moisture is important because it is essential for vegetation growth. It is the principal constituent of growing plants, it is required for photosynthesis, it is the solvent and carrier of food and nutrition for plant growth, it regulates soil temperature, it is important for microorganisms in the soil which require water for their metabolic activities and also soil forming processes and weathering is depending on water. In a broader view, the knowledge of soil moisture is important because it controls the partitioning of incoming solar radiation into sensible and latent heat fluxes and it controls the partitioning of precipitation into infiltration and surface runoff. How can we measure soil moisture? There are many ways of measuring soil moisture. So you can directly measure soil moisture in the field by taking soil samples or you can do indirect measurements by measuring a specific variable which allows conclusions on the moisture content in the soil. And one of these principles or methods we want to show you today is the TDR principle and TDR stands for Time Domain Reflectometry. This can be used for measuring moisture content of natural media like soils and it is basically relying on the measurement of the propagation velocity of an electromagnetic energy pulse in the soil and relies on the fact that the transit time measurement of an electric signal is determined by the average moisture constant along the so-called waveguides of the sensor. So what are the waveguides? Here we have a small overview of a setup for doing time domain reflectometry measurements. So it consists mainly of a pulse generator, an oscilloscope and in the soil we have three so-called probes or waveguides which are metal sticks and they are conducting materials. How does time domain reflectometry work? So in the first step the pulse generator is generating an electric pulse which is traveling along cables to the soil sensor and in the second step this pulse is reaching the point where the waveguides are inserted into the soil and this will generate a signal response which can be seen on the oscilloscope. Then the signal or the electric pulse is traveling along the waveguides into the soil and as soon as the signal is reaching the end of the waveguides another response signal is generated and can be seen on the oscilloscope. The TDR measurement produced two responses which can be seen in the oscilloscope and the propagation speed is determined from the time elapsed between these two responses. So to say something about moisture content we need to know the propagation speed of the pulse along the waveguides. To get this speed we have the two responses which can be seen on the oscilloscope and we know the time which has been elapsed between these two points on the oscilloscope and when knowing the propagation speed we can draw conclusions on the relative permittivity and this gives us information about the average moisture content and as a rule of thumb you can say that the smaller the propagation speed the higher the relative permittivity and also the moisture content in the soil. Now that we know how the general setup of a TDR device looks like we also want to know what is happening behind the scenes so what is actually happening and the waveguides we are inserting into the soil are electric conductors and when a current flows through a conductor there are electric and magnetic fields around this conductor and so these electromagnetic waves are traveling through a medium and in any case they will lose energy and this loss of energy can be called attenuation. The soil can be seen as a so-called lossy dielectric medium so that means that we look at the so-called bulk properties of the medium to characterize its properties and we are not looking at the properties of its individual constituents so we are looking at this medium as a whole and the properties of such a medium used to describe the interactions of the electromagnetic field and the medium are first the electric permittivity, second the magnetic permeability and third the electric conductivity so at the moment we can just neglect properties number two and three so the magnetic permeability and the conductivity and we only have a look at the electric permittivity. The electric permittivity is usually upperweighted with the greek letter epsilon and it defines if and how an electric field can pass or travel through a medium and it is also a measure of the electric polarizability of a material so here we have a little formula which says epsilon equals epsilon r and epsilon zero, epsilon zero is the so-called relative permittivity of free space or vacuum and epsilon r is the relative permittivity we actually are interested in so for a medium which absorbs the energy from a wave we have to use a complex number to represent the electric constant and this is shown on this slide so here we have the complex electric permittivity and it consists of a real part and an imaginary part where the imaginary part describes the energy losses and the electric constant we are actually interested in is represented by the real part of this formula. So the electric constant can be seen as a material constant which is a unitless constant so we have no unit like meters or kilograms or whatever and at 1 gigahertz and 20 degrees Celsius the electric constant of water is 80 and the electric constant of soil is 2.6 and when we add water to a soil the electric constant will increase tremendously and this is also the reason why radar systems are actually that sensitive to moisture content. At the right hand side there is a table with some typical values of geoelectric constants for materials we find in nature and literature you will often read at radar frequencies when something is written about the dielectric constant so what does it mean? It actually means that the dielectric constant depends on the frequency of the electromagnetic waves or pulses and this is also shown in the diagram you can see at the right hand side in this case for water at a temperature of 20 degrees and we see that the dielectric and the real part of the dielectric constant decreases rapidly with increasing frequency. To come back to our TDR measurement there is another relation which is important and this is shown in this diagram here at the left hand side and this relation is the relation between the wave velocity and the dielectric constant. The higher the dielectric constant the slower the wave velocity and when knowing this we can actually draw conclusions on the moisture content of the soil. So now we know what is going on behind the scenes when doing time domain reflectometry so I want to summarize it in three points so electromagnetic waves can propagate a natural media like a soil, the propagation speed depends on the dielectric properties of this material and when we know the propagation speed we can draw conclusions on the water contents via the dielectric constant. So the question is now why does adding water to a soil has such a pronounced effect on the dielectric constant? And this is because of the special properties of water. So water is a molecule consisting of oxygen and hydrogen H2O and water is a so called polar molecule and this leads to the fact that water behaves like a dipole. So what is a dipole? A dipole is a pair of equal and opposite electric charges on magnetic poles of opposite sign separated especially by a small distance. So on this slide we have a figure and this shows how the water molecules acting as dipoles are oriented if no electromagnetic field is applied. In this case they are randomly arranged and as soon there is an electromagnetic field impinging on this water surface, on the soil surface, they will react on an external electric field and they will align with the field lines. And as soon as we remove the field or switch it off they will swing back. This reaction of the dipoles on the presence of an electromagnetic field leads to the fact that we can measure a hydroelectric constant and for open water surfaces we have the fact that the incident electromagnetic waves are almost completely rejected. So when talking about this so called orientation polarization of water there are two important facts we need to know. The first one is that this polarization effect depends on temperature. It means if we have ice or temperatures below zero the dipoles are immobilized so they cannot follow any electromagnetic fields and we also cannot measure soil moisture with radar or with a TDR sensor. The second important fact we need to know is that the polarization also depends on frequency. The dipoles swinging back and forth can only follow the electromagnetic field up to a certain frequency and this frequency is called the relaxation frequency. Above this threshold the dipoles cannot follow the electromagnetic field oscillations any longer. And this relaxation frequency in the case of water is around 10 GHz.

content: Ein Effekt, über den wir hier sprechen müssen in der Radarfernerkundung, ist der sogenannte Speckle-Effekt. Speckle als solches führt dazu, dass die Radarbilder, die Rückstrahlintensitäten, angezeigt als Sigma-Null-Werte, verrauscht aussehen. Also verrauscht im Sinne, wir haben Helligkeitsunterschiede, kleinräumige Helligkeitsunterschiede, die einen ähnlichen Eindruck vermitteln wie Fotografien, aufgenommen mit einem sehr sehr hohen ISO-Wert. Und auf dem ersten Blick scheint auch dieses in Anführungsstrichen Rauschen nicht direkt was mit der Landoberfläche zu tun zu haben. Also es erstreckt sich über das gesamte Bild, auch wenn das nicht völlig korrekt ist. Dennoch müssen wir hier Abstand davon nehmen, bei Speckle von Rauschen zu sprechen. Es ist ein gänzlich anderer Prozess, der dahinter steckt. Zunächst ist Speckle für die meisten Untersuchungen hinderlich und man versucht dementsprechend auch Speckle zu beseitigen. Dafür hat man speziell angefertigte Speckle-Filter, die die Statistik des Speckles berücksichtigen, entwickelt. Das funktioniert am allerbesten, wenn ich multitemporale Aufnahmen verwende. Das heißt, dasselbe Gebiet wird wiederholt aufgezeichnet und wenn ich Aufnahmen ab einer Anzahl 10, 15 Stück habe, wird es auch langsam sinnvoll, einen solchen multitemporalen Speckle-Filter ins Spiel zu bringen und die Daten entsprechend zu filtern und letzten Endes zu glätten. Die einfachste Möglichkeit Speckle zu filtern wäre ein Tiefpass-Filter beziehungsweise ein Mittelwert-Filter. Dem sollte man auf jeden Fall den Vorzug geben gegenüber einem Median-Filter, weil der Median-Filter völlig andere Statistiken annimmt und der Mittelwert-Filter wird für Radardaten eher besser funktionieren. Aber letzten Endes, wie gesagt, es gibt dezidierte Speckle-Filter, die auf jeden Fall deutlich bessere Filterergebnisse liefern, weil sie in der Lage sind, Kanten zu erkennen und nicht über Kanten hinweg zu filtern. Eine andere Möglichkeit, Speckle zu reduzieren, wäre auch schon während der Datenprozessierung, während der Vorprozessierung der Daten, indem ich mit Multilook-Faktoren arbeite, die eben in der Lage sind, tatsächlich auch die Menge des Speckles zu reduzieren. Aber was ist eigentlich dieser Speckle? Wie kommt der zustande und wie könnte ich vielleicht sogar ein System konstruieren, ein Radarsystem, um von vornherein Speckle zu eliminieren? Stellen wir uns mal eine Rückstreuzelle vor, das heißt eine Auflösungszelle, in der letzten Endes mehrere Streuobjekte vorhanden sein können. Nehmen wir mal diesen Notizblock hier als Auflösungszelle mit einer Dimension X, einer Dimension Y. Wie in diesem Beispiel handelt es sich nicht um eine quadratische Zelle, das ist auch der gängigste Fall bei der Radarfernerkundung. Und in dieser Auflösungszelle befinden sich mehrere Objekte, nehmen wir mal diese Legosteine hier, die dafür sorgen, dass eine gewisse Rückstreuintensität erzeugt wird. Also jedes dieser Objekte streut die einfallende elektromagnetische Strahlung zurück. Das sind jetzt vier identische Streuobjekte. Das hieße eigentlich, dass jedes dieser Objekte auf eine gleiche Art und Weise auch die einfallende Energie zurück zum Sensor streut. Wichtig ist jedoch zu verstehen, dass nicht nur die Energiemenge dieser einzelnen Streuobjekte sich auf die Radarrückstreuung der gesamten Auflösungszelle auswirkt, sondern auch der Abstand der Objekte zum Radarsensor als auch der Abstand dieser Objekte zueinander. Weil, und das ist das Besondere bei der Radarfernerkundung, wir es mit kohärenten Systemen zu tun haben. Kohärente Systeme arbeiten mit einer Wellenlänge, mit einer Polarisation und letzten Endes können wir deswegen die Phaseninformationen nicht vernachlässigen, wenn es um die Auswertung von Radardaten geht. Dazu werde ich jetzt mal eine kleine Skizze an das Whiteboard anzeichnen, um das Ganze etwas zu verdeutlichen. Ich reduziere jetzt mal unseren experimentellen Aufbau ein wenig, indem ich zwei Streuobjekte entferne und zwei Streuobjekte übrig lasse. Wir gehen mal davon aus, die beiden Streuobjekte sind tatsächlich identisch. Beide Streuobjekte sorgen für die gleiche Energiemenge jeweils und das gesamte andere Areal innerhalb dieser Auflösungszelle sorgt für vernachlässigbar wenig Rückstreuenergie. Jetzt kann ich also für jedes dieser beiden Streuobjekte im Prinzip eine Sinuskurve anzeichnen, die die zurückgestreute Energie symbolisieren soll. Wir haben hier einmal die Amplitude, also die Menge der zurückgestreuten Energie. Die sollte bei beiden Objekten gleich sein, weil es sich um die gleichen Objekte handelt. Also wir haben zweimal die gleiche Amplitude, die wir hier feststellen können und in dem Fall sogar auch die gleiche Phase. Die gleiche Phase ist letzten Endes nichts anderes als der Wert, den unsere Sinuskurve auf der x-Achse hat, der jeweils zwischen 0 und 2 Pi gemessen werden kann. Eine genauere Messung der Phase bzw. über Phasenwerte größer als 2 Pi hinaus ist mit Radarsystemen schlicht und einfach nicht möglich. Wir messen also die Phase immer zwischen 0 und 2 Pi und zwar als Zeitpunkt, zu dem unsere elektromagnetische Welle auf unsere Radarantenne trifft. Jetzt können wir also, wenn wir zwei Streuobjekte haben, unterschiedliche Fälle in der Addition dieser beiden Amplituden erhalten. Einerseits kann wie in diesem Fall die Phase gleich sein. Wir haben in beiden Fällen eine mehr oder weniger identische Phase. Das heißt, die Wellenberge addieren sich und die Wellentäler addieren sich auch und das Ganze erzeugt eine zurückgestreute Energiemenge, die genau doppelt so groß ist wie die eines einzelnen Streuers. Dies würde beispielsweise genau dann auftreten, wenn beide Streuobjekte den gleichen Abstand zum Sender haben. Jetzt ist es allerdings möglich, dass die Streuobjekte anders angeordnet sind, dass beispielsweise ein Objekt sich näher am Sensor befindet oder das andere weiter weg und das verändert die ganze Situation. Im Extremfall wird es sich eines unserer Objekte genau eine halbe Phasenlänge näher oder weiter entfernt vom Sensor befinden und zwar wäre das jetzt dieser rote Fall. Das heißt, die Amplitude wäre nach wie vor gleich, allerdings hätten wir hier einen Phasenversatz von genau einer halben Wellenlänge und das führt dazu, dass bei kohärenten Systemen, Radar wie gesagt ist kohärent, es zu einer Auslöschung dieser Phasen kommt. Streuobjekt 1 in schwarz, Streuobjekt 2 in rot und letzten Endes herrscht hier negative Interferenz. Wir haben also eine vollständige Phasenauslöschung, obwohl sich in diesem Pixel zwei Objekte befinden, die tatsächlich Radarrückstreuung generieren. Das heißt schlussendlich, ich kann, obwohl sich zwei identische Objekte innerhalb einer Auflösungszelle befinden, völlig unterschiedliche Rückstreuintensitäten erlangen, je nachdem wie diese Objekte zueinander angeordnet sind und das verursacht den Speckel. Wichtig zu verstehen ist jedoch auch, dass eine zweite Aufnahme mit identischen Aufnahmebedingungen, das heißt die Objekte haben sich nicht bewegt, der Sensor steht wieder exakt an derselben Stelle, arbeitet mit derselben Wellenlänge, dass in meinem Bild wieder exakt derselbe Speckel entsteht. Speckel ist in dem Fall nicht zufällig, Speckel ist deterministisch. Das ist sehr, sehr wichtig zu verstehen.

content: Let's journey into open science to see how FAIR, open data, and open source software work in a real research project. We'll look at input data, analysis, result generation, and scientific publication. The Clear Snow Project is a great example of open science. Clear snow describes past, present, and future snow cover in the European Alps. The results are obtained by combining in situ observations, remote sensing data, and climate models. The first step is to gather the input data. Satellite and climate data help us analyze snow cover across the Alps. Fortunately, this data is already openly available, perfect for reproducibility. However, this is not the case for snow depth station data across all Alpine countries. To gather from more than 2,000 stations across different countries and provinces and to harmonize this data is very labor-intensive. Keep that data set in mind. Everything needed to reproduce the project results is publicly available on GitHub. Anybody interested can download the code and reproduce the results. Additionally, an R software package has been developed to simplify working with EuroCortex regional climate models, EuroCortex-R. Remember those snow station measurements we were talking about earlier? Well, that data set has been made fair and open. The data set is registered on OpenAIR, an open science catalog, and it has its digital object identifier, so it's findable. It's hosted on Zenodo, an open data portal, so it's accessible. It uses machine-readable formats, in this case, annotated CSV files, so it's interoperable. And it has an open license attached to it, CCx4.0, so it's reusable. Finally, the scientific publication is the last step of the open science journey. The clear snow paper has been published in the open access journal, the Cryosphere, made available as preprint, and its data and code have been linked to the publication. This means there are no barriers in finding, reading, and seeing what other researchers think about this publication or in reproducing its results. Hard work for sake of opening research pays off. The clear snow project has already had more than 4,200 unique downloads and a vast number of citations. This means it has helped as many people in their research projects. The extra work to open up these results is really worth it. Now that you know your way around, it's your turn to follow the journey for your own research.

metadata.video_title: The Open Science Journey

content: The radar equation is probably the most important equation in the context of radar remote sensing. It is a fundamental constraint on how radar systems operate. In a LiDAR context you will also come across the LiDAR equation which is very similar but it has some subtle differences because you're using lasers and you're in the optical and infrared domain and therefore you have atmospheric conditions to worry about. In a radar context we don't have to worry about transmission through the atmosphere so that won't appear in the radar equation. What the radar equation does is estimates how much energy you will get back to your sensor if you transmit a certain amount of energy. So the key thing is that it is measuring a return signal so the intensity of the echo that comes back. Fundamentally that is proportional to how much energy we transmit so the first parameter in the radar equation is the transmitted power. If we transmit twice as much power we'll get twice as much signal back. So it's a linear relationship between the transmitted and the received power. A key term that we use is isotropic. We refer to isotropic transmitters as being a transmitter that sends energy equally in all directions. An isotropic scatterer scatters energy equally in all directions. It means the incoming wave will scatter with the object and then it scatters the energy equally in all directions. Typically many objects won't do that. Many objects will actually scatter preferentially into one direction. A key term is isotropic. An isotropic radiator is a transmitter that will transmit energy equally in all directions. An isotropic scatterer is an object that if a wave is interacting with an object it will scatter the energy equally in all directions. It's a bit of an idealised type of scatterer. Most real objects will actually scatter preferentially into one direction or another. Sometimes they'll preferentially scatter the energy directly back to the satellite like a trihedral corner reflector. The key thing about an isotropic scatterer is that it's scattering equally in all directions and that is a convenient approximation, especially when we don't know what the nature of the target is. If our antenna was an isotropic transmitter, so if it transmitted energy equally in all directions, it would lose energy in proportion to the surface area of the sphere, so the expanding sphere of energy. It would lose energy as a factor of 4 pi r squared. It's a square law. It's a loss in proportion to the distance squared. Our antennas are much better than an isotropic radiator. Our antennas are able to direct a lot of that energy into a small, narrow range of directions. We characterise that with the antenna gain. The antenna gain is a factor that determines how much of that energy is directed into the direction towards the target rather than isotropically. By the time that energy of our transmitted pulse reaches our target, it will have dropped off in energy by 4 pi r squared. So r is the distance between our antenna and the target that we're trying to measure. Now the target will scatter some of that energy back towards the antenna. We'll talk about that in a second. But the key thing is that the energy that is re-scattered by our target on its way back to the antenna is also diminished in intensity by 1 over 4 pi r squared. Now because we don't know anything about our target, we use the symbol sigma to represent the property of our target in terms of how good it is at scattering. That's our radar cross-section. What we do to characterise our radar cross-section is that we say, well, if it was a hole in space that collected a certain amount of energy that was arriving at the target and then redistributed it isotropically, how much energy would get back to our sensor? And because we're considering our target, we're characterising our target as a hole in space that's collecting that energy, we use a cross-section and we talk about the radar cross-section as our measure of how good this scatterer is at scattering energy. Our radar cross-section is then in units of metres squared. It's an area. When we're looking at the Earth's surface, what we do is normalise that over the area that we're measuring. So it becomes an area, the radar cross-section, divided by an area, so the area of ground over which we're measuring. And so we end up with a unitless measure called the normalised radar cross-section or sigma naught. And that's the way that we characterise our target. So we're making an assumption that it's an isotropic scatterer. And we make that assumption simply because we don't know exactly what the scatterer is like. We don't know if it is a particularly special scatterer, if it directs energy in one particular direction or not. We have to make a broad assumption that it's an isotropic scatterer. Now when the energy from our target is on its way back to the sensor, it's losing energy again by 1 over 4 pi r squared. And then when it gets to the antenna, we have a parameter called the antenna effective area, which characterises how good the antenna is at collecting that energy coming back. The result of all that is that our radar equation essentially says that the amount of energy that we get back, so the power received is equal to the power transmitted times the gain times the antenna effective area times our target property, this sigma or sigma naught. And that's all divided by 16 times pi squared times r to the fourth. So our energy is dropping off with r to the fourth. That's an incredible loss of energy. So even over a short distance, let's say 100 metres, on its way to the target, it's already dropped by a factor of 10,000. By the time it comes back, we've now lost another 10,000. One of the key things that the radar equation tells us is that the amount of energy that we get back in a radar system is extremely small. It drops off very, very quickly with distance. The important thing about the radar equation is that it tells us that the amount of energy that we get back is very, very small. It drops off very, very quickly with distance. What we end up with in the radar equation is that it tells us that the power received drops off as one over the distance to the power of four. That's a very, very rapid drop off. Even with just 100 metres, you're already 10,000 times less in signal by the time you reach the target. And by the time it gets back to the antenna, it's another 10,000 times smaller. And so you're 100 million times less intense in terms of the echo compared to the signal that you transmitted. Now scale that up to 600 kilometres of an Earth observation satellite with a radar system. And you can see that the amount of signal that you will get back from a radar transmitter is extremely small. That puts certain limits on how radar systems can work in terms of how much energy you transmit compared to how much energy you get back. It means that radar satellites are really restricted in terms of how much power and the amount of power that they need. Because the radar equation tells us that the amount of signal that we will get back is so small, is that it puts certain limits on what a radar system can do. It means we have to generate pulses that have very high powers. And that puts some limits on terms of the peak power and the length of time that the pulse that we might transmit. In a satellite context, your only source of power is solar panels. And so it's really important that you can collect as much energy as possible from the sun. Unlike passive sensors, radar sensors have to transmit their own energy. And therefore they have to collect as much energy as possible so that they can transmit high intensity signals to ensure that you get a signal back that you can measure. The good news is that the technology is good enough to actually transmit high powered pulses, so that you can still detect the echoes coming back from the Earth's surface, even at hundreds of kilometres in orbit above the Earth. The radar equation is one of the most important equations in radar remote sensing. It determines how much energy we get back in an echo, depending on how much energy we transmit. So let's imagine that we're here at our radar system, and over there is our target that we're trying to measure. So one of the key things is how we transmit the energy. A very simple system would transmit energy isotropically, so equally in all directions. But we have an antenna that's a bit better than that. It can direct some of the energy or more of the energy towards our target. And we characterise that as the function g, which is the antenna gain. So the key thing is we transmit a power, so Pt is our transmitted power, and it's focused by the antenna with the factor of the antenna gain. Then the signal, travelling at the speed of light, travels all the way down towards our target. And as it travels towards our target, the energy is lost as a function of the surface area of a sphere. And that drops off as 1 over 4 pi r squared. So this is our target. The energy from the antenna has dropped off considerably, so it's now dropped off by a factor of 4 pi r squared, surface area of a sphere. Some of that energy is going to interact with our target and be returned to the antenna. Because we don't know anything about our target, we have to assume that it's an isotropic scatter, that it takes the energy and it scatters it equally in all directions. Now the way that we characterise our target is to say that, well, with this big pulse of energy coming over past the target, how big a hole in space would you have that could collect the energy and then redistribute it equally in all directions, some of which would go back to the antenna? And it's this area that we talk about as the radar cross-section, measured as an area in units of metre squared. When we're measuring the Earth's surface, what we do is normalise that to the area over which we're measuring. So it becomes an area divided by an area, and so we end up with a unitless quality known as the normalised radar cross-section, or sigma naught. This energy is then redistributed and makes its way back. Some of the energy makes its way back to the radar system. The energy on its way back to the radar system is also losing energy at a rate of 1 over 4 pi r squared. So it's losing energy as a square law as well. By the time that energy gets back to our antenna, the antenna then captures some of that energy, and that's where it's characterised by the antenna's effective area. The net effect of the radar equation is that we lose energy at a rate of 1 over r to the fourth.
